rows per identifier: p50=2 p90=4 p99=7 max=15
identifiers with more than 10 rows: 195
quarters per identifier: max 4  rows per identifier and quarter: max 8


def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, privacy_unit: tuple[dp.Metric, Any]) -> dp.Context:
    """The documentation's context: approximate differential privacy, split evenly over four queries."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=privacy_unit,  # dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT") below
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=DELTA),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
        margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=MAX_LENGTH)],
    )
budget per query: epsilon=0.25 delta=2.5e-09

try:
    context.query().filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99).select(hours().dp.mean(HOURS)).summarize()
    untruncated = "accepted"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    untruncated = reason(err)
mean without truncation: A step in your query is not recognized at this time: "DF ["PIDENT", "YEAR", "QUARTER", "SEX", ...]; PROJECT */8 COLUMNS". ""If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.2 Truncating each person’s rows
The documentation’s first query is the mean of HWUSUAL, the hours usually worked, without the code 99 for “not applicable”. The mean needs public bounds on the hours, 0 to 80, and a bound on the rows per person. truncate_per_group(10) gives that bound: it keeps at most ten random rows per identifier before the aggregation.
mean_query = (
    context.query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)  # 99 means "not applicable"
    .truncate_per_group(ROWS_PER_IDENTIFIER)  # at most 10 rows per identifier, chosen at random
    .select(hours().dp.mean(HOURS))
)
mean_summary = mean_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
dp_mean = mean_query.release().collect().item()
mean, 10 rows per identifier: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=6,400.0 95% accuracy=19,173.2
mean, 10 rows per identifier: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2
A mean is released as a sum and a count, as in Essential statistics. The two split the query’s share, so each gets \(\varepsilon/8\). One person now moves the count by at most ten rows, so the count’s sensitivity is 10, and its scale is 10 over \(\varepsilon/8\). Each row adds at most 80 hours to the sum, so the sum’s sensitivity and scale are 80 times larger. Truncation and clipping are the two ways to make a sensitivity finite, and the full edition’s chapter on sensitivity derives what each does to the answer.
Under the unit of 36 contributions, the same mean gets scales of 23,040 and 288. The price of the truncation is bias, because the mean leaves out the rows after the tenth. On this file the price is nothing: the truncation drops 20 rows of about 1.5 million.
rows with HWUSUAL not 99: 1,496,192 by 809,710 identifiers
identifiers with more than 10 such rows: 18  rows dropped: 20
unit of 36 contributions, no identifier: scales 23,040.0, 288.0
The keep argument says which rows remain. The default, "sample", keeps a random ten: its plan numbers each identifier’s rows in a shuffled order and keeps the numbers below ten. With "first" or "last" the numbering follows the file’s order, which is cheaper but biased when the order means something. A SortBy keeps the rows that sort first by an expression, such as ILOSTAT, the employment status. No choice changes the scales, because the bound of ten rows holds whichever rows remain.
truncate_per_group(10) plan: FILTER [(0.int_range([len().cast(Int64)]).shuffle().over([col("PIDENT")])) < (10)]
keep=first: scales 6,400.0, 80.0
keep=last: scales 6,400.0, 80.0
keep=SortBy(ILOSTAT): scales 6,400.0, 80.0
ILOSTAT values among them: [1]
The last line shows that every row after the filter has ILOSTAT equal to 1, so here the sort changes nothing.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
section: 5.3 Truncating the groups a person touches
text:
5.3 Truncating the groups a person touches
The second query is a table with one row per quarter, grouped by QUARTER and YEAR, with the number of responses and the sum of their hours. Now the noise depends on two bounds: the rows that a person adds to one group, and the number of groups that a person touches. The counts change by at most the first bound in each of at most the second number of groups. So the total sensitivity is the product of the two. The full edition derives this in its section on contribution bounding.
So the query truncates twice. truncate_per_group(1, by=quarterly) keeps one row per identifier and quarter, and truncate_num_groups(10, by=quarterly) keeps at most ten quarters per identifier. Without the second truncation the library refuses the query, and this time the message says what is missing. (The script cuts the message’s suggestion, whose column order changes from run to run.)
per quarter without truncate_num_groups: num_groups (None), total contributions (None), and per_group (Some(1)) are not sufficiently well-defined. This is likely due to a missing truncation earlier in the data pipeline.
The query below is the documentation’s, except for keep="first" in the group truncation, for a reason given below.
quarter_query = (
    context.query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)
    .truncate_per_group(1, by=QUARTERLY)  # one row per identifier and quarter
    .truncate_num_groups(GROUPS_PER_IDENTIFIER, by=QUARTERLY, keep="first")  # at most 10 quarters each
    .group_by(QUARTERLY)
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), hours().dp.sum(HOURS))
)
quarter_summary = quarter_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
quarters_hat = quarter_query.release().collect()
per quarter, 10 quarters per identifier: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2 threshold=1,714
per quarter, 10 quarters per identifier: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=6,400.0 95% accuracy=19,173.2
The scales are the ones of the mean, because one row in each of ten quarters is again ten rows per person. The query gives no public keys, so the library releases a quarter only if its noisy count is above the threshold, as in Grouping. Every quarter has at least 27,228 responses, so all 36 appear.
Version 0.16.0 has two problems with truncate_num_groups. With the default, keep="sample", the query passes summarize and release spends its share, but collect fails inside Polars.
sample_query = grouped_query(context, keep="sample")  # the same table, with the default keep
sample_summary = sample_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
released = sample_query.release()  # spends the query's share of the budget
try:
    released.collect()
    sample_outcome = "collected"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    sample_outcome = reason(err)
keep=sample: summarize scales 80.0, 6,400.0; collect: multiple fields with name 'QUARTER' found
shares spent after the failed collect: 4 of 4
The share is gone, because the budget is spent when the measurement is built. But Polars checks a plan without the data, so explain() before release shows the same error at no cost, as on this toy frame.
import opendp.prelude as dp
import polars as pl

dp.enable_features("contrib")
toy = pl.LazyFrame({"PIDENT": [7, 7, 7], "YEAR": [2005] * 3, "QUARTER": [1, 2, 3], "HWUSUAL": [35.0, 36.0, 37.0]})
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=toy,
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT"),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-8),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=100)],
)
quarterly = [pl.col("QUARTER"), pl.col("YEAR")]
query = context.query().truncate_per_group(1, by=quarterly).truncate_num_groups(10, by=quarterly)
query = query.group_by(quarterly).agg(dp.len(signed=True))
print(f"{query.summarize()['scale'].item():.1f}")  # 10.0
try:
    query.explain()
except pl.exceptions.DuplicateError as err:
    print(str(err).splitlines()[0])  # multiple fields with name 'QUARTER' found
The second problem is with keep="first" and keep="last", which run. Their plan keeps the ranks of an identifier’s quarters below the number that you ask for. But Polars counts ranks from one, so the truncation keeps one group fewer than asked, as the two numberings show.
import polars as pl

toy = pl.DataFrame({"PIDENT": [7, 7, 7], "YEAR": [2005] * 3, "QUARTER": [1, 2, 3]})
quarterly = [pl.col("QUARTER"), pl.col("YEAR")]
numbered = toy.with_columns(
    index=pl.int_range(pl.len()).over("PIDENT"),  # what truncate_per_group compares with k
    rank=pl.struct(quarterly).rank("dense").over("PIDENT"),  # what truncate_num_groups compares with k
)
print(numbered["index"].to_list(), numbered["rank"].to_list())  # [0, 1, 2] [1, 2, 3]
No identifier spans more than four quarters, so the script measures the effect at a smaller k. A request for four keeps at most three quarters, so the 13,948 identifiers with four quarters lose one. A request for five keeps all four, at the scale and threshold of five.
truncate_num_groups(10, keep=first) plan: FILTER [(col("QUARTER").as_struct([col("YEAR")]).rank().over([col("PIDENT")])) < (10)]
identifier-quarters after the filter: 1,241,896  identifiers with 4 quarters: 13,948
truncate_num_groups(4, keep=first): keeps at most 3 quarters, 1,227,948 identifier-quarters; scale 32.0 threshold 657
truncate_num_groups(5, keep=first): keeps at most 4 quarters, 1,241,896 identifier-quarters; scale 40.0 threshold 830
So in version 0.16.0, ask for one group more than you want to keep, and accept the noise of that larger number. The guarantee is safe either way, because the library calibrates to the number asked for. The estimate is not, because the dropped group is always the last in sort order. The practitioner edition’s release workflow avoids the call for these reasons.
Put the truncations of a query next to each other, with the group truncation last before the aggregation. With a filter between them, the library calls the truncation’s own expression unrecognized.
a filter between the two truncations: Expr is not recognized at this time: dyn int: 0.int_range([len()]).shuffle().over([col("PIDENT"), col("QUARTER"), col("YEAR")]). If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.4 One row per person
For a mean, there is a better method than ten rows per person. Group by the identifier first, aggregate each person’s rows to one row with any Polars expression, and take the private mean of those rows. After the group-by, no identifier owns more than one row.
person_query = (
    context.query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)
    .group_by("PIDENT")  # one row per identifier: the truncation
    .agg(pl.col("HWUSUAL").mean())  # any expression may summarize the person's rows
    .select(hours().dp.mean(HOURS))
)
person_summary = person_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
dp_person_mean = person_query.release().collect().item()
mean of one row per identifier: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=640.0 95% accuracy=1,917.8
mean of one row per identifier: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=8.0 95% accuracy=24.5
The count’s sensitivity is now 1 and the sum’s is 80, so both scales are a tenth of the scales with ten rows. And no row is dropped.
But the question changes. The first query averaged over responses, so a person with four responses counted four times. This one averages each person’s own average, so every person counts once, which gives 37.24 hours against 37.64. The cast to an integer then truncates each person’s mean towards zero, which lowers the true value to 37.10. With an error bar of about 0.0035 hours, the choice of what to average matters far more than the noise.
true mean of one row per identifier: 37.0970  (before the cast to int: 37.2359; all rows: 37.6393)
per-identifier mean error bar at the true size: 0.0035

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.5 Bounds in the privacy unit
The unit can also hold finer knowledge, as a list of dp.polars.Bound objects. Each names its grouping, a bound on identifiers per group and a bound on the groups that one person touches. The documentation’s example is data merged from two sources that assigned identifiers separately. A person can then appear under two identifiers, which would double the noise, but never under two in the same quarter.
two_sources = dp.unit_of(
    contributions=[
        dp.polars.Bound(per_group=2),  # a person may appear under two identifiers
        dp.polars.Bound(by=QUARTERLY, per_group=1),  # but under one identifier in any quarter
    ],
    identifier="PIDENT",
)
bounded = make_context(frame, two_sources)
bounded_query = grouped_query(bounded, keep="first", k=5)  # each identifier may affect up to 5 quarters
bounded_summary = bounded_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
bounded_hat = bounded_query.release().collect()
two identifiers, one per quarter, 5 quarters: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2 threshold=1,714
two identifiers, one per quarter, 5 quarters: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=6,400.0 95% accuracy=19,173.2
one identifier as a bound, 5 quarters: scales 40.0, 3,200.0
The query keeps one row per identifier and quarter, and five quarters per identifier. Two identifiers times five quarters is ten rows per person, so the scale is 80 again. The second bound tells the library that the two identifiers never meet in one quarter, so one person adds at most one row to any quarter. It does not lower the count’s scale, because the ten rows can still fall in ten different quarters. With a single identifier as the bound, the same query gets half the scale.
A bound in the unit can also have num_groups, the number of groups that a person touches. Then the query needs no truncate_num_groups, and a promise of ten quarters gives the same scale as the truncation at ten. But the library enforces a truncation, while it takes a bound on trust. The script makes a promise that this file breaks, that no identifier spans more than three quarters, and the release goes through with no complaint.
promised = dp.unit_of(
    contributions=[
        dp.polars.Bound(per_group=1),
        dp.polars.Bound(by=QUARTERLY, per_group=1, num_groups=3),  # a promise: at most 3 quarters each
    ],
    identifier="PIDENT",
)
promise_query = (
    make_context(frame, promised)
    .query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)
    .truncate_per_group(1, by=QUARTERLY)  # no truncate_num_groups: the unit already bounds the quarters
    .group_by(QUARTERLY)
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), hours().dp.sum(HOURS))
)
promise_summary = promise_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
promise_hat = promise_query.release().collect()
num_groups=10 promised in the unit: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2 threshold=1,714
num_groups=3 promised in the unit: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=24.0 95% accuracy=72.4 threshold=486
num_groups=3 promised in the unit: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=1,920.0 95% accuracy=5,752.3
identifiers that break the promise of 3 quarters: 13,948
The noise is calibrated for three quarters, but 13,948 identifiers have four. For those people the privacy loss is above the declared \(\varepsilon\), and nothing in the output says so. So truncate in the query, where the library enforces the bound. Declare a bound in the unit only when no truncation can express it, as with the two identifiers above, which no filter can recognize as one person. The same advice applies to values: clip them in the query, and do not declare their range in the input domain. Assessing utility and choosing the noise returns to bounds per group with Gaussian noise, whose scale depends on them differently.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.6 The check against the truth
The data are public, so the script computes what each query would return without noise, with its own seeded random ten rows for the first mean. The quarters’ true values use the first row of each identifier in each quarter, while the release keeps a random row. So the check is exact for the counts and approximate for the hours.
true mean, 10 rows per identifier: 37.6393  (1,496,172 rows)
true per quarter (first row per identifier and quarter): 36 quarters, rows from 27,228 to 41,868
true 2005Q1: rows 29,561  hours 1,110,610
true 2005Q2: rows 29,406  hours 1,106,170
true 2005Q3: rows 28,364  hours 1,070,826
true 2005Q4: rows 28,681  hours 1,080,009
Here are the releases of one run. Each mean’s error bar comes from the bars of its sum and its count, and holds whenever both hold.
released (one run):
  mean, 10 rows per identifier: 37.6366  (true 37.6393, within 0.0189 with probability at least 0.9)
  per quarter: 36 quarters released; rows within their 95% accuracy: 36 of 36; hours: 35 of 36
  2005Q1: rows 29,644  hours 1,105,518
  2005Q2: rows 29,460  hours 1,098,965
  2005Q3: rows 28,244  hours 1,063,846
  2005Q4: rows 28,645  hours 1,087,028
  mean of one row per identifier: 37.0970  (true 37.0970, within 0.0035 with probability at least 0.9)
  two bounds, 5 quarters: 36 quarters released; rows within four times their 95% accuracy: 36 of 36
  num_groups=3 promised: 36 quarters released; rows within four times their 95% accuracy: 36 of 36
The means are within their bars, and so are the quarters’ counts and all but one of their sums. A bar of 95% predicts about that many misses for 36 values. The test checks the two means within three times their bars and the 36 quarters within four times theirs, so a correct run almost never fails it.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.7 Summary



Table 5.1: The calls of identifier truncation and bounds, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT")
The privacy unit is every row of one identifier
contributions now counts identifiers; the rows per person are bounded by the query


A query with no truncation
Refused, with a message that blames the data scan
On a context with an identifier, every statistic sits behind a truncation


truncate_per_group(k, keep=...)
Keeps at most k rows per identifier, and per group with by
"sample" is unbiased; "first", "last" and SortBy are cheaper or deliberate, and biased when order matters


truncate_num_groups(k, by=...)
Keeps at most k groups per identifier
In 0.16.0, "sample" fails at collect after the budget is spent, and "first" keeps k - 1 groups; call explain() before release()


Truncations in a query
Must sit next to each other, the group truncation last
A filter between them makes the query unrecognized


group_by("PIDENT").agg(...) before a statistic
One row per person, so the sensitivity is that of one row
The best choice for a mean, if the mean over people is the one you want


dp.polars.Bound(by, per_group, num_groups) in unit_of
Finer bounds on identifiers per group and groups per person
A promise the library trusts; a person who breaks it loses more than \(\varepsilon\)


Truncate or declare
The query enforces a truncation; the unit declares a bound
Truncate, and declare only what no truncation can express

5.8 References

Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (2006): sensitivity and the Laplace mechanism.
Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina and Vassilvitskii, “Bounding User Contributions: A Bias-Variance Trade-off in Differential Privacy” (2019): why truncating a person’s rows trades bias for variance.
Wilson, Zhang, Lam, Desfontaines, Simmons-Marengo and Gipson, “Differentially Private SQL with Bounded User Contribution” (2020): bounding rows per group and groups per user in grouped queries.
The full edition’s chapters on sensitivity and user-level privacy derive the results this chapter states.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.1 Prepare inside the query
Survey data rarely arrive in the form that a statistic needs. Hours of work come as floats, with 99 for “not applicable” and a null for a missing answer. The date of a response is in two integer columns. So before you release anything, you cast, fill, clip, filter and recode. This chapter is about where that work happens. OpenDP reads the whole lazy query before it runs, preparation included, and accounts for every step. So the preparation belongs inside the query, where the guarantee covers it.
The chapter follows the documentation’s tutorial on preparing microdata, its page on data types and its pages on expressions. You see which Polars contexts and expressions OpenDP allows, what it changes about them, and how it tracks nulls, undefined floats and bounds. The chapter ends with a worked preparation of the Labour Force Survey (LFS), for the mean difference between actual and usual hours of work.
The script opendp_preparing_microdata.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with Polars 1.36.1. The noise scales, error bars, thresholds, error messages and true values that it prints are the same on every run. The released counts and mean are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so this page shows them in one block marked as one run.
A context on a Polars LazyFrame reads only the frame’s schema, which the library treats as public, and touches the data only at a release. OpenDP parses each query, a lazy plan, into a chain of transformations before anything runs, as Transformations explains. For each step, the library finds how much one person’s rows can change the output. So a filter or a fill in the middle of the plan is part of the accounting.
Preparation before the context is different, because the library then sees only the prepared frame, and its guarantee is about that frame. A fixed function of each row, such as a renamed column or a date parsed with a known format, leaves every person with the same rows. Then the guarantee still holds, but the claim is yours, because the library did not check it. A step that reads the data is worse. An imputation by the column’s own mean, a bound at its maximum or a filter at a quantile carries information about everyone into the release, outside the accounting. Before the context, use only public facts, such as the schema, the code book and the published bound on the sample’s size.
The context has the privacy unit of the data and the context, up to 36 rows per person, and that chapter’s bound on the rows. The budget is approximate differential privacy, with a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) of 1 and a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\), split evenly over four queries.
The schema line is all that the context knows about the data at this point, and it assumes that any column can hold nulls.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dp.Context:
    """The documentation's context: 36 rows per person, (epsilon = 1, delta = 1e-7) split evenly over 4 queries."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=DELTA),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
        margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=MAX_LENGTH)],  # public: a bound on the number of rows
    )
privacy unit: (SymmetricDistance(), 36)
privacy loss: (Approximate(MaxDivergence), (1.0, 1e-07))
budget per query: epsilon=0.25 delta=2.5e-08
schema: PIDENT=Int64  YEAR=Int64  QUARTER=Int64  SEX=Int64  AGE=Float64  HWUSUAL=Float64  HWACTUAL=Float64  ILOSTAT=Int64

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.2 Columns, filters and groups
Polars applies an expression in one of five contexts, and OpenDP puts them in two groups. Expressions in .select and .agg can change the number and the order of rows, because an aggregation does exactly that. Expressions in .with_columns, .filter and .group_by must be row-by-row: a function applied to each row on its own. The reason is the privacy unit. A row-by-row expression keeps each person’s rows their own, so 36 rows in gives 36 rows out. An expression that sorted or shifted the column would mix people’s rows, and the library could not say what one person changes.
The documentation’s first example adds a column with .with_columns and groups on it. The row-by-row expression cut puts the usual hours into bands at fixed breaks, and replaces HWUSUAL with its bin. The labels of the bins depend only on the breaks, so they are public and can be the keys.
def binned_counts(context: dp.Context) -> LazyFrameQuery:
    """How many responses fall in each band of usual hours: a row-by-row `cut`, then a count per bin."""
    labels = pl.Series("HWUSUAL", cut_labels(BREAKS, left_closed=True), dtype=pl.Categorical)
    return (
        lazy_query(context)
        .with_columns(pl.col("HWUSUAL").cut(breaks=BREAKS, left_closed=True))  # shadows HWUSUAL with its bin
        .group_by("HWUSUAL")
        .agg(dp.len(signed=True))
        .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame([labels]))  # the bin labels are public, so no threshold is needed
    )
binned counts: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
without keys: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 threshold=2,973
true bins: null=20,819  [-inf, 0)=0  [0, 20)=89,495  [20, 40)=908,061  [40, 60)=406,947  [60, 80)=78,469  [80, 98)=13,220  [98, inf)=2,294,921
The scale is the 36 rows that one person can add to a bin, divided by the query’s share of the budget. With the keys, every bin is released, including the empty one below zero, whose signed count can be negative. Without the keys, the library must learn from the data which bins exist, so the query has a threshold, as in Grouping. The rows with a null HWUSUAL fall in a null bin that is not among the keys, so no release has them. Also, a margin that you declared about HWUSUAL applies to the original column, and the new column has none.
A .filter removes rows with a boolean row-by-row expression, such as the documentation’s filter on the code 99 before a sum. A filter keeps most of what the margins say. But it discards any invariant about the group keys and sizes, which were facts about the data before the filter. A filter also tells the library nothing about what remains: a column filtered to non-null values is still nullable in its domain.
filtered sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=11,520.00 95% accuracy=34,511.3
The last context of the tutorial is a .group_by and .agg before the private aggregation. In the documentation’s version of sample and aggregate, the rows go into 1,000 groups by PIDENT, and the query releases the mean of each group’s minimum usual hours. Any expression can go in that inner .agg, but the price is noise. The script prints the scales of the mean on the context above, and with a Bound from Identifier truncation and bounds that puts each person’s rows in one group.
sample and aggregate: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=17,280.00
sample and aggregate: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=576.00
one group per person: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=480.00
one group per person: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=16.00
The first context does not know that a person’s rows share a PIDENT, so it allows for 36 changed groups. Even with the bound, the inner aggregation doubles the noise, because a changed group counts as one value removed and another added.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.3 The types OpenDP tracks
OpenDP assumes that every column can hold nulls until an expression proves otherwise. It also keeps domain descriptors for each column: facts about its values that later aggregations need. For a number it tracks lower and upper bounds, which a .clip sets and some later steps drop. The supported integers are the signed ones and the unsigned ones of 32 and 64 bits, so a UInt8 column is refused. A float column also records whether its values can be NaN, the float for an undefined number, so a float sum needs both .fill_null and .fill_nan. Booleans and strings have no descriptors.
A categorical column stores an integer code per value, with a table of labels, and two things about that table depend on the data. An expression that could add or remove a category, such as .fill_null, makes Polars rewrite the codes and warn, a side effect that depends on the data. And the codes follow the order in which the values first appear, so a group-by on them would show the order of the rows. So the library refuses both. An Enum column fixes its categories in the schema, so neither problem occurs, and neither does it with cut, whose encoding depends only on the breaks.
import polars as pl
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
status = ["working", "absent", "other"] * 100
unit, loss = dp.unit_of(contributions=1), dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-7)


def context_for(column: pl.Series) -> dp.Context:
    return dp.Context.compositor(data=pl.LazyFrame([column]), privacy_unit=unit, privacy_loss=loss, split_evenly_over=1)


categorical = context_for(pl.Series("status", status, dtype=pl.Categorical))
try:
    categorical.query().group_by("status").agg(dp.len(signed=True)).summarize()
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(err.message)  # Categories are data-dependent, which may reveal sensitive record ordering. Cast status to string before grouping.
enum = context_for(pl.Series("status", status, dtype=pl.Enum(["working", "absent", "other"])))
print(f"{enum.query().group_by('status').agg(dp.len(signed=True)).summarize()['scale'].item():.4f}")  # 1.0000
The error names the fix, a cast to string, and the enum query goes through. Dates, datetimes and times are also supported, with one time zone per datetime column.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.4 Casting, filling and clipping
The documentation’s reason to cast is the float sum. OpenDP accounts for the rounding error of float addition, and on many rows with wide bounds that term shows in the noise scale. The script sums the usual hours both ways.
def hours_sum(context: dp.Context, as_integers: bool) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """The noise scale of a sum of usual hours, on the float column or after casting it to integers."""
    usual: Any = pl.col("HWUSUAL")  # typed Any: OpenDP adds the `.dp` namespace to expressions at run time
    column = usual.cast(int) if as_integers else usual
    return lazy_query(context).select(column.dp.sum(HOUR_BOUNDS)).summarize(alpha=0.05)
float sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Float Laplace, scale=14,405.18 95% accuracy=43,154.1
integer sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=14,400.00 95% accuracy=43,139.0
On integers the scale is exactly 36 times the upper bound of 100 over the share of the budget, and on floats it is a little more. A cast has one more effect. In Polars, a value that cannot be converted raises an error, which depends on the data, so OpenDP makes a failed cast return a null. So every cast column is nullable, and a statistic on it needs a .fill_null first.
import polars as pl
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=pl.LazyFrame({"hours": ["40", "35", "n/a"] * 100}),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=1000)],
)
hours = pl.col("hours").cast(int)  # OpenDP turns "n/a" into a null instead of raising an error
try:
    context.query().select(hours.clip(0, 80).sum().dp.noise()).summarize()
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(err.message)  # input data (hours) might contain nulls. Preprocess your data with `.fill_null`.
query = context.query().select(hours.fill_null(0).clip(0, 80).sum().dp.noise())
print(query.summarize()["scale"].item())  # 80.0
The .dp.sum of the earlier chapters adds the imputation and the clip for you. The snippet instead prepares the column by hand and adds noise to a plain .sum, to show what the library checks. The sum needs the bounds that a .clip sets, because without bounds one person could move the sum by any amount. But .fill_null and .fill_nan drop the bounds, so fill first, then clip. The script runs the same preparation on the survey in .with_columns, and tries the wrong orders.
def prepared_sum(context: dp.Context, steps: pl.Expr) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """A sum with noise on a column prepared in with_columns: OpenDP checks the steps left it non-null and bounded."""
    total: Any = pl.col("HWUSUAL").sum()
    return lazy_query(context).with_columns(steps).select(total.dp.noise()).summarize()
prepared sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=14,400.00
cast without fill_null: input data (HWUSUAL) might contain nulls. Preprocess your data with `.fill_null`.
clip before fill_null: input domain must consist of bounded data. Either specify bounds in the input domain or use make_clamp.
fill_null before fill_nan: input data (HWUSUAL) might contain nans. Preprocess your data with `.fill_nan`.
float prepared sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Float Laplace, scale=14,405.18
The fill value can also come from another column, such as the actual hours for missing usual hours. Then the column and the fill must both be row-by-row, so that their rows line up, and the fill must have no nulls.
filled from a column: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=14,400.00
filled from a nullable column: fill expression must not be nullable
The expressions .drop_nulls and .drop_nans remove rows and change the column’s length, so the library forbids them in a row-by-row context.
drop_nulls in with_columns: drop_nulls is not allowed in a row-by-row context
Recoding has two forms. The expression .replace swaps listed values and keeps the type. The expression .replace_strict maps every value and can change the type, so an unmapped value takes the default. The documentation says that OpenDP sets a missing default to null, but version 0.16.0 does not. On a toy column of three codes with a mapping for two, summarize accepts the query, but release fails. So give replace_strict a default yourself.
replace_strict without default: summarize scale=2.0; release: InvalidOperation(ErrString("incomplete mapping specified for `replace_strict`\n\nHint: Pass a `default` value to set unmapped values."))
replace_strict with default: released keys one other two

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.5 Predicates and arithmetic
OpenDP accepts the comparison, conjunction and arithmetic operators of Polars, as row-by-row expressions. Both sides of a binary operator must be row-by-row even inside .select or .agg, because a length mismatch would raise an error that depends on the data. Tests such as is_null and is_nan are row-by-row too, and they build filters and grouping columns. The documentation counts the respondents over retirement age with a group-by on a comparison.
def over_retirement_age(context: dp.Context) -> LazyFrameQuery:
    """How many responses come from people over 64: a boolean expression as the grouping column."""
    return (
        lazy_query(context)
        .group_by(pl.col("AGE") > RETIREMENT_AGE)
        .agg(dp.len(signed=True))
        .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"AGE": [True, False]}))  # a null age is in neither group and is dropped
    )
over 64: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
true over 64: true=1,190,845  false=2,620,832  null=255
A comparison with a null is null, so the 255 rows without an age form a third group that the keys leave out. The grouped form answers both halves of the question for the price of one.
Version 0.16.0 does not support two operators that you might want. It refuses is_in, membership in a list, so write the test as a disjunction of equalities. The script counts the employed in this way.
is_in: IsIn { nulls_equal: false } is not currently supported
employed: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
The other is the absolute value, in Section 6.8.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.6 Strings and dates
Of the string expressions, OpenDP supports only parsing into a temporal type, with .str.strptime and its variants to_date, to_datetime and to_time. The format argument is mandatory, because a format inferred from the data could change with one person’s rows. Nanosecond datetimes are refused, because the parser can panic on some inputs, an error that depends on the data.
to_date without format: format must be specified; otherwise Polars will attempt to infer the format from the data, resulting in an unstable transformation
nanosecond datetime: Nanoseconds are not currently supported due to potential panics when parsing inputs. Please open an issue on the OpenDP repository if you would find this functionality useful. Otherwise, consider parsing into micro- or millisecond datetimes instead.
The survey has no date column, only YEAR and QUARTER. The documentation builds one with concat_str before the context, because the library refuses concatenation inside a query.
concat_str: Expr is not recognized at this time: ConcatHorizontal { delimiter: "-", ignore_nulls: false }. If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.
But arithmetic is supported, so you can build the date inside the query. The year times 100 plus three times the quarter gives an integer such as 200503. As a string, it parses with the format %Y%m into the first day of the quarter’s last month. The .dt expressions then read the components of the date, from the year to the day.
def quarter_end() -> pl.Expr:
    """The last month of the quarter as a date, built from YEAR and QUARTER and parsed with a fixed format."""
    year_month = pl.col("YEAR") * 100 + pl.col("QUARTER") * 3  # 2005 and 1 become 200503
    return year_month.cast(str).str.to_date(format="%Y%m")


def responses_per_month(context: dp.Context) -> LazyFrameQuery:
    """How many responses carry each quarter-end month, read off the parsed date."""
    return (
        lazy_query(context)
        .with_columns(DATE=quarter_end())
        .group_by(pl.col("DATE").dt.month().alias("MONTH"))
        .agg(dp.len(signed=True))
        .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"MONTH": pl.Series(QUARTER_END_MONTHS, dtype=pl.Int8)}))
    )
first dates: 2005 Q1 -> 2005-03-01  2005 Q2 -> 2005-06-01
per month: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
true per month: 3=953,695  6=958,396  9=933,257  12=966,584
Every quarter ends in one of four public months, so they are the keys, with no threshold. The keys have the type Int8, because they must match the type that .dt.month returns.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
section: 6.7 A worked preparation: hours lost to absence
text:
6.7 A worked preparation: hours lost to absence
The statistic is the mean difference between the hours that a person with a job actually worked in the survey week and the hours that they usually work. A negative mean means that holidays, illness and short weeks outweigh overtime. Each step of the preparation is a decision about the data, inside the query. First the query keeps ILOSTAT equal to 1, working for pay or profit. It casts both hour columns to integers, for the integer noise of Section 6.4. It fills the usual hours with 0. Then it keeps the rows whose usual hours are known, without 0 for hours that vary and 99 for not applicable.
The fill comes before the filter because a filter proves nothing to the library (Section 6.2). After the filter, no null usual hours remain, but the column is still nullable in its domain. And the next step uses it as a fill value, which must not be nullable. That step gives a row without actual hours its usual hours, so its difference is zero, the least informative choice. Last, the query clips the difference to public bounds of plus or minus 40 hours, because a sum needs bounds. The full range of plus or minus 80 would double the noise.
def prepare[Frame: (LazyFrameQuery, pl.LazyFrame)](frame: Frame) -> Frame:
    """The rows of people who work, with their usual hours known, and the hours they lost that week, clipped."""
    low, high = LOST_BOUNDS
    return (
        frame.filter(pl.col("ILOSTAT") == 1)  # working for pay or profit
        .with_columns(pl.col("HWUSUAL").cast(int).fill_null(0), pl.col("HWACTUAL").cast(int))
        .filter((pl.col("HWUSUAL") > 0) & (pl.col("HWUSUAL") < 99))  # 0 is "varies", 99 "not applicable"
        .with_columns(pl.col("HWACTUAL").fill_null(pl.col("HWUSUAL")))  # unknown actual hours: assume the usual
        .with_columns(LOST=(pl.col("HWACTUAL") - pl.col("HWUSUAL")).clip(low, high))
    )
The function takes a query or a plain LazyFrame, so the release and the check use one preparation. The query ends in pl.col("LOST").dp.mean(LOST_BOUNDS), and summarize shows what the mean costs.
hours lost: LOST Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=11,520.00 95% accuracy=34,511.3
hours lost: LOST Length, Integer Laplace, scale=288.00 95% accuracy=863.3
hours lost, bounds (-80, 80): LOST Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=23,040.00 95% accuracy=69,022.2
A mean is a noisy sum over a noisy count, which split the query’s share of the budget. So the sum’s scale is 36 rows times the bound of 40, over an eighth of the budget. With bounds of plus or minus 80, the sum’s scale doubles, so the clip is a trade: a narrower bound gives less noise and more bias. The full edition’s chapter on sensitivity derives how the bounds of a sum set its sensitivity.
The survey is public, so the script measures the bias, which on real data you can do only with a public or historical copy.
true prepared rows: 1,490,113  true sum of hours lost: -9,289,648  true mean: -6.2342
rows the clip changes: 42,830 (2.874%)  mean without the clip: -6.5319
mean error bar at 95%: 0.0268
The clip changes under three percent of the rows. But these rows move the true mean from -6.53 hours to -6.23, a bias of about a third of an hour. The noise is far smaller. The script turns the two accuracies into an error bar for the mean: the sum’s bar plus the mean times the count’s bar, all over the count. It comes to 0.027 hours. So on this many rows, the clip limits the result, not the noise.
released (one run):
  bins: [-inf, 0)=-129  [0, 20)=89,491  [20, 40)=907,895  [40, 60)=406,594  [60, 80)=78,436  [80, 98)=13,452  [98, inf)=2,294,708
  over 64: true=1,190,894  false=2,620,771
  per month: 3=953,684  6=958,313  9=933,077  12=966,807
  hours lost: mean -6.2147  (true -6.2342, within 0.0268 with probability 0.95)
budget spent: 4 of 4 queries
Every count is within its bar of about 432, and the empty bin is negative, as a signed count can be. The mean is within its bar of the clipped truth. The four releases used the four shares. Assessing utility and choosing the noise takes the error bars further.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
section: 6.8 What a refused expression looks like
text:
6.8 What a refused expression looks like
An expression that OpenDP cannot parse raises an OpenDPException, with a variant and a message, when you build the query and before it reads any data. The absolute value of the difference in hours is an example.
abs: Expr is not recognized at this time: [(col("HWACTUAL")) - (col("HWUSUAL"))].abs(). If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.
The messages on this page are of two kinds. “Not recognized at this time” means that nobody has implemented the expression yet, as with concat_str and abs. The other messages state a rule, such as a mandatory format or a fill that must not be nullable, and each names its fix inside the query. For an expression without an implementation, rewrite it with supported operators if you can, as is_in became a disjunction. If not, apply it before the context, but only if it is a fixed function of each row. Then state that step with the release, because the library did not check it.

text:

Nissim, Raskhodnikova and Smith, “Smooth Sensitivity and Sampling in Private Data Analysis” (2007): the sample and aggregate framework behind the stable group_by/agg.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
text:
7.1 What an accuracy statement means
Every query in the earlier chapters printed a scale and an accuracy before its release. This chapter is about how to read those two numbers and change them. An accuracy is the half-width of an error bar: with a stated probability, the released value is within that distance of the value that the noise was added to. OpenDP converts a noise scale to an accuracy and back, so you can find what a target error bar costs before you spend anything.
The second half of the chapter is about which noise to add. Under pure differential privacy (DP) the context adds Laplace noise, and under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) it adds Gaussian noise. One argument of dp.loss_of selects between them. The choice matters most when one person’s records fall in many groups. Then Gaussian noise is calibrated to a sensitivity that grows with the square root of the number of groups, not with the number itself. On the survey, this cuts the noise on a quarterly count six-fold, but only under zCDP.
The script opendp_utility_and_noise.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 against the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample of the earlier chapters. The conversions, scales, accuracies, thresholds and budgets that it prints are the same on every run. The released counts and the means of a small clamping experiment are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so this page shows them in blocks marked as one run.
The documentation gives a template to read the accuracy functions. At a given scale, the released value is within the accuracy of the true value at a significance level \(\alpha\), that is, with confidence \((1 - \alpha) \times 100\%\). Every accuracy in this book has \(\alpha = 0.05\), so about one release in twenty is outside its error bar. A smaller \(\alpha\) gives a wider bar, as Essential statistics showed at \(\alpha = 0.01\).
The module opendp.accuracy has eight conversion functions, which the prelude gives under dp. Four convert a Laplace or Gaussian scale to an accuracy and back, and the other four, with discrete_ in their names, do the same for integer noise. The documentation’s example asks for the Gaussian scale at which a release is within 2 of its input with 95% confidence.
The continuous functions are closed forms. For Laplace noise, the accuracy is the scale times \(\ln(1/\alpha)\). For Gaussian noise, it is the scale times the two-sided normal quantile, about 1.96 at the usual level. The discrete functions sum the probabilities of the integer noise, so a discrete Gaussian accuracy is a whole number. Use the discrete ones for counts, because OpenDP adds integer noise to an integer, and the continuous ones for sums and means of floats. At a scale of 180 the difference is small, and summarize always uses the correct one.
The error bar is about the noise and nothing else, and this is the most frequent mistake in how people read one. The accuracy functions say how far the release can be from the input to the noise mechanism: the statistic of the data after every preparation step. A clip into public bounds, an imputed constant, a truncation of a person’s rows and a resize all change that input. The error bar says nothing about the gap between the input and the quantity that you want. Those gaps are biases, which no number of repeated releases removes. The practitioner edition’s release workflow measures one, where truncation and clipping keep about half of the revenue.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
section: 7.2 A target error bar on the survey
text:
7.2 A target error bar on the survey
Suppose you want the count of survey responses within 100 of the truth with 95% confidence. Start from the count that Essential statistics released, with \(\varepsilon = 1\) split evenly over five queries. The excerpt summarizes it again, and then asks the discrete Laplace conversion for the scale that the target needs.
laplace = laplace_context(frame, EPSILON)
count_laplace = laplace.query().select(dp.len(signed=True))
laplace_summary = count_laplace.summarize(alpha=ALPHA)
scale_needed = float(dp.accuracy_to_discrete_laplacian_scale(accuracy=TARGET, alpha=ALPHA))
epsilon_needed = CONTRIBUTIONS / scale_needed  # the Laplace scale is the sensitivity over epsilon
laplace count: Integer Laplace scale=180 95% accuracy=539.731
budget per query: epsilon=0.2000
error bar relative to the true count: 0.014%
discrete laplace scale for accuracy 100: 33.2152
epsilon that scale needs at sensitivity 36: 1.0838  (5.42 times the share)
The scale of 180 is the sensitivity over the share of 0.2, with a sensitivity of 36 from the privacy unit. The target needs a scale of 33.2, which costs more than the whole budget on this one query. So a bar of 100 is not available at this budget. But a bar of 0.014% of the true count is already small for a headline figure.
The conversion also gives the exchange rate. The Laplace scale is the sensitivity over \(\varepsilon\), and the accuracy is proportional to the scale, so half the error bar costs twice the budget. At \(\varepsilon = 2\) the same query gets half the scale.
laplace count at epsilon 2: Integer Laplace scale=90 95% accuracy=270.115
The bar is not exactly half, because the discrete conversion rounds the integer noise, but the rule of thumb holds. The full edition’s chapter on the Laplace mechanism derives the scale and the tail bound behind the conversion.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
section: 7.3 Laplace under pure DP, Gaussian under zCDP
text:
7.3 Laplace under pure DP, Gaussian under zCDP
OpenDP chooses the noise from the kind of budget. With dp.loss_of(epsilon=...), the guarantee is pure DP and the context adds Laplace noise. With dp.loss_of(rho=...), the guarantee is zCDP and the context adds Gaussian noise. Nothing else in a query changes, unless the query names a distribution. So the script’s two context functions differ only in the budget line.
def laplace_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, epsilon: float) -> dp.Context:
    """Pure differential privacy: the context adds Laplace noise."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=epsilon),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
    )


def gaussian_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, rho: float, delta: float | None = None) -> dp.Context:
    """Zero-concentrated differential privacy: the context adds Gaussian noise."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=delta),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
    )
The privacy loss is the log of how much more likely an output is with a person in the data than without. Pure DP bounds it by \(\varepsilon\) in the worst case. Zero-concentrated DP bounds it on average. A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when its privacy loss has mean at most \(\rho\) and tails no heavier than those of a normal variable with variance \(2\rho\). The Gaussian mechanism fits this definition exactly, and budgets in \(\rho\) add up across queries as budgets in \(\varepsilon\) do. The full edition’s chapter on concentrated DP derives all of this. The documentation’s Gaussian page repeats the count under \(\rho = 0.1\), split over the same five queries.
gaussian = gaussian_context(frame, RHO)
count_gaussian = gaussian.query().select(dp.len(signed=True))
gaussian_summary = count_gaussian.summarize(alpha=ALPHA)
privacy loss: (ZeroConcentratedDivergence, 0.1)
gaussian count: Integer Gaussian scale=180 95% accuracy=354
budget per query: rho=0.0200  sqrt(2 rho)=0.2000
continuous gaussian accuracy at scale 180: 352.7935
The scale is again 180, on purpose. Write \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise, which OpenDP calls its scale, and \(\Delta\) for the sensitivity. The mechanism is \(\Delta^2 / (2\sigma^2)\)-zCDP, so the context sets the scale to the sensitivity over \(\sqrt{2\rho}\). With a share of \(\rho = 0.02\), that root is 0.2, the Laplace share. At equal scale the Gaussian bar is narrower, because Gaussian tails fall faster. But equal scale is not equal privacy: Section 7.5 converts this share of \(\rho\) to an \(\varepsilon\) of about 1, five times the Laplace share.
The exchange rate also differs. The Gaussian scale is the sensitivity over \(\sqrt{2\rho}\), so half the error bar costs four times \(\rho\), as the script confirms at \(\rho = 0.4\).
gaussian count at rho 0.4: Integer Gaussian scale=90 95% accuracy=177
So on a single count, Gaussian noise under zCDP gives no gain. Its advantage is on a query that answers many things at once.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
section: 7.4 One person in many groups: L1 against L2
text:
7.4 One person in many groups: L1 against L2
A grouped count returns a vector, one number per group, and the noise is calibrated to how far one person can move the whole vector. Laplace noise measures that distance in the \(L_1\) norm, the sum of the changes across groups. Gaussian noise measures it in the \(L_2\) norm, the root of the sum of their squares. Between opposite corners of a unit square, the \(L_1\) distance is 2 and the \(L_2\) distance is \(\sqrt 2\). In \(d\) dimensions they become \(d\) and \(\sqrt d\).
On the survey, a person answers at most once per quarter, so their 36 records fall in 36 different groups of year and quarter, each changed by one. The \(L_1\) distance between the two count vectors is 36, but the \(L_2\) distance is \(\sqrt{36} = 6\). If you do not tell the library, it must assume that all 36 records are in one group, and then both distances are 36. The dp.polars.Bound of Identifier truncation and bounds tells it.
def bounded_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, privacy_loss: tuple[Measure, Any]) -> dp.Context:
    """A budget of either kind, with the privacy unit also bounded to one record per year and quarter."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(
            contributions=[
                dp.polars.Bound(by=[], per_group=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # at most 36 records overall
                dp.polars.Bound(by=["YEAR", "QUARTER"], per_group=1),  # and one in each year and quarter
            ]
        ),
        privacy_loss=privacy_loss,
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
    )
The budget now has a \(\delta\), because the query has no public keys. So the context releases only the groups whose noisy count passes a threshold, as in Grouping. The script summarizes the quarterly count three ways: under zCDP with 36 contributions only, with the bound per group, and with that bound under pure DP.
bounded = bounded_context(frame, dp.loss_of(rho=RHO, delta=DELTA))
count_by_quarter = bounded.query().group_by("YEAR", "QUARTER").agg(dp.len(signed=True))
grouped_summary = count_by_quarter.summarize(alpha=ALPHA)
privacy loss with a threshold: (Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence), (0.1, 1e-07))
grouped count, 36 contributions: Integer Gaussian scale=180 95% accuracy=354 threshold=1133
grouped count, 1 per year and quarter: Integer Gaussian scale=30 95% accuracy=60 threshold=184
grouped count, 1 per year and quarter, pure DP: Integer Laplace scale=180 95% accuracy=539.731 threshold=3712
true groups: 36  smallest 82,504  largest 131,656
The bound per group cuts the Gaussian scale from 180 to 30, the factor of six above, and the threshold falls with it. Under pure DP the bound changes nothing, because the \(L_1\) distance is 36 either way. The thresholds are far below the smallest quarterly count, so every group is released, with an error bar of 60. The full edition’s chapter on the two mechanisms proves why Gaussian noise scales with the \(L_2\) sensitivity.
In general, when a person’s records spread thinly over many groups, the \(L_2\) sensitivity is far below the \(L_1\) one. Then Gaussian noise under zCDP is the correct tool. But the gain needs a bound per group. If public knowledge cannot justify the bound, enforce it with a truncation first.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
text:
7.5 Stating the guarantee in epsilon
A budget in \(\rho\) is convenient for accounting, but most readers of a release do not know it. OpenDP converts it to the usual pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with two combinators, which Combinators covers. The first, make_zCDP_to_approxDP, turns a zCDP guarantee into a curve of \(\varepsilon\) against \(\delta\). The second, make_fix_delta, picks a \(\delta\) on that curve. The script applies them to a Gaussian measurement whose scale makes a sensitivity of 1 cost exactly \(\rho\).
def epsilon_of_rho(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The epsilon that OpenDP's conversion gives for rho-zCDP at delta, read off a Gaussian measurement."""
    space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
    gaussian = dp.m.make_gaussian(*space, scale=1 / math.sqrt(2 * rho))  # sensitivity 1 at this scale is rho-zCDP
    approx = dp.c.make_fix_delta(dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(gaussian), delta)
    epsilon, _ = approx.map(1.0)
    return float(epsilon)
rho=0.1 at delta=1e-07: epsilon=2.3484
closed form rho + 2 sqrt(rho ln(1/delta)): 2.6391
rho=0.02 (one query) at delta=1e-07: epsilon=0.9951
the whole context converted: epsilon=2.3484 delta=1e-07
At \(\delta = 10^{-7}\), the whole budget of \(\rho = 0.1\) is worth \(\varepsilon = 2.35\), and one query’s share is worth about \(\varepsilon = 1\). The textbook conversion is \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho \ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{7.1}\] which gives 2.64 here. OpenDP’s smaller number comes from a tighter conversion over the orders of the Rényi divergence, which the full edition’s chapter on conversions derives. You can also convert a whole context: its accountant attribute is the measurement that composes every query. The two combinators on it give the same 2.35, the number to write in the release’s statement.
You choose this \(\delta\). Keep it far below one over the number of people, because a \(\delta\) of that size allows a mechanism that publishes one person’s record. With 1.7 million people, \(10^{-7}\) is defensible. This \(\delta\) is a conversion cost, separate from the \(\delta\) of the threshold in the grouped query, so a release that needs both must budget both.
The Gaussian count’s summary said 354, while the continuous conversion at the same scale gives 352.79. The context adds a discrete Gaussian to an integer count, so it reports the discrete accuracy, as Measurements explains. So to recompute an accuracy from a scale, use the discrete function for counts.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
text:
7.6 Signed and unsigned counts
Every count on this page has signed=True, because of bias. A noisy count can be negative when the true count is small, and OpenDP used to raise such a value to zero. In version 0.16.0, signed=True casts the count to a signed integer before the noise, so a negative result stays. With signed=False or no argument, the result is clamped at zero, and without the argument the library warns that the default will change.
For a single small cell, clamping even reduces the error. The problem is a sum of counts. A clamped count can be too high but never too low, so each small cell is biased upwards. A total over hundreds of cells adds up those biases. The OpenDP cookbook shows this on a table of 400 mostly empty cells. The clamped total is too high on every repetition, while the signed total is correct on average.
You can clamp a signed release afterwards for display, because that is free post-processing. So release signed counts whenever anyone might sum, average or model them. The script shows the bias on a small scale. It counts an empty frame a thousand times at a fixed Gaussian scale of 30, through the framework API without a context, which suits toy data only.
def mean_noisy_count_of_nobody(signed: bool, scale: float, repeats: int) -> float:
    """The mean of `repeats` noisy counts of an empty frame, at a fixed Gaussian scale, signed or clamped at zero."""
    empty = pl.LazyFrame(schema={"A": pl.Int32})
    domain = dp.with_margin(
        dp.lazyframe_domain([dp.series_domain("A", dp.atom_domain(T="i32"))]),
        dp.polars.Margin(by=[], max_length=1000),
    )
    count = dp.m.make_private_lazyframe(
        domain, dp.symmetric_distance(), dp.zero_concentrated_divergence(), empty.select(dp.len(signed=signed)), scale
    )
    return sum(int(count(empty).collect().item()) for _ in range(repeats)) / repeats

The unsigned mean is near 12, the mean of the positive half of a Gaussian of scale 30, and no number of repetitions brings it down. A table of empty cells released unsigned has that 12 in every cell.

7.7 Which noise to choose
The choice depends on what you release and to whom you must explain it, as Table 7.1 shows.



Table 7.1: Which noise to choose, by what is released.










Situation
Noise and budget
Why




One count, sum or mean, and a guarantee in pure \(\varepsilon\)
Laplace under dp.loss_of(epsilon=...)
The guarantee has no \(\delta\) and is the easiest to state


A grouped table where a person touches many groups
Gaussian under dp.loss_of(rho=..., delta=...) with a Bound per group
The \(L_2\) sensitivity grows with the root of the number of groups


Many queries composed into one release
Gaussian under zCDP
Budgets in \(\rho\) add up tightly and convert once at the end


A release that others will analyse assuming normal errors
Gaussian
The noise is normal, so standard intervals apply


A guarantee that must be reported as \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)
Either; convert \(\rho\) with make_zCDP_to_approxDP and make_fix_delta
OpenDP’s conversion is tighter than the closed form


Counts that anyone might add up
Either, with signed=True
Clamping at zero biases totals upward






Two cautions go with the table. Gaussian noise cannot satisfy pure DP, so a policy that demands \(\delta = 0\) rules it out. And the gain from the \(L_2\) sensitivity exists only when the library knows how a person’s records spread across groups. So the bound per group is part of the choice.

title: The framework
text:
Every query that the Context API ran in the previous parts was built from a few pieces, and this part shows those pieces. OpenDP’s framework describes a private computation as a chain of two kinds of object. A transformation maps data to data, and its stability bounds how much its output can change when its input changes. A measurement maps data to a random release, and its privacy bounds how much the distribution of the release can change. In a chain, these promises pass from one step to the next, and when you compose measurements, their privacy losses add up. So when you can read these objects, you can see exactly which guarantee a query carries. You can also build queries that the Context API does not offer, and check a claim that someone else makes.
The first chapter gives the vocabulary: domains, metrics and measures, and the two maps that carry the promises. The next three build the pieces in order: the data-to-data steps, the mechanisms that add noise or select, and the combinators that chain and compose them. The last chapter covers the tools around the pieces and shows how the Context API maps onto them.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




A framework to understand differential privacy
What are domains, metrics, measures, transformations and measurements, and what does each promise?


Transformations
How do I build and chain the data-to-data steps, and how does stability flow through them?


Measurements
Which mechanisms does OpenDP offer, and how do I calibrate each one?


Combinators
How do I compose measurements, convert between privacy measures, and account adaptively?


Utilities and the Context API inside
How do types, parameter search and serialization work, and what does a context do under the hood?






At the end of this part, you can build a private query from its pieces and read the guarantee of any chain with map and check. You can also explain what the Context API does when it resolves a query.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.1 Two kinds of object
Every query of the first two parts used the Context API, which chose a noise scale, spent a share of the budget and refused a query above it. Under that API, OpenDP describes a private computation with two kinds of object. A transformation maps data to data, and it promises how far apart its outputs can be when its inputs are close. A measurement maps data to a random release, and it promises how far apart the distributions of its releases can be. Each promise is a map from an input distance to an output distance, and differential privacy (DP) in OpenDP is the bookkeeping of such maps. At the end of the chapter, you can read the guarantee of any OpenDP object from its fields and its map.
The script opendp_framework.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0. Its sum example uses the HWUSUAL column of the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample as a list of integers, and its workflow uses the first chapter’s hundred toy scores. The domains, metrics, measures, maps, scales and error bars are the same on every run. The released values change, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the page shows them in one block marked as one run.
The first chapter built a Laplace measurement without saying what came back. The documentation’s example is the same mechanism with a scale of 5. It uses make_laplace, which takes the domain and the metric as its first two arguments instead of through >>.
What comes back is a Measurement, and the script reads its fields.
A transformation and a measurement share four fields. The function is the computation, it accepts the input_domain and produces the output_domain, and the input_metric gives the distance between two inputs. The last two fields differ, because a transformation is deterministic while a measurement is random. A transformation’s output is data, so it has an output_metric and a stability map, which bounds the distance between two outputs from a bound on the distance between the inputs. A measurement’s output is a random draw, so it has an output_measure and a privacy map, which bounds the distance between two output distributions.
So the Laplace measurement accepts one finite float, compares two inputs by their absolute difference, and compares two output distributions by the max divergence, which \(\varepsilon\) bounds. The documentation states the two promises in one shape. A transformation is (d_in, d_out)-stable when inputs at most d_in apart give outputs at most d_out apart. A measurement is (d_in, d_out)-differentially private when the same inputs give output distributions at most d_out apart. The sections below take the parts of these sentences in turn.

text:
def laplace_measurement(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Laplace noise of the given scale on one finite float, compared by absolute distance, under pure DP."""
    return dp.m.make_laplace(
        dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False),  # input domain: any float that is not NaN
        dp.absolute_distance(T=float),  # input metric: |a - b|, the units of the sensitivity
        scale=scale,
    )
