title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.2 Non-adaptive composition
When you run the sum and the count on the same data, you spend both budgets. Basic composition says that the total is the sum of the parts. So an \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP release and an \(\varepsilon_2\)-DP release on the same data are together \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP (the full edition’s chapter on properties). The combinator make_composition builds that rule into one measurement, which runs every part and returns the releases as a list.
both = dp.c.make_composition([shortcut, count])  # one measurement that releases the sum and the count
print(f"composition: map(1)={both.map(1):.1f}  parts: {shortcut.map(1):.1f} + {count.map(1):.1f}")
composition: map(1)=3.0  parts: 2.0 + 1.0
composition output measure: MaxDivergence
The parts must agree on their input domain, input metric and output measure. A composition is a statement about one dataset, one notion of neighbours and one measure of privacy. It is non-adaptive, because every part is fixed before the data are seen.
The same combinator composes measurements under other measures, with each measure’s own rule. Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) measures privacy by one parameter \(\rho\), which bounds the Rényi divergence between the output distributions on neighbours at every order. Under zCDP the parameters add like \(\varepsilon\) (the full edition’s chapter on concentrated DP). The Gaussian sum at scale 5 has \(\rho = 2\), the Gaussian count at scale 1 has \(\rho = 0.5\), and the composition reports their sum.
zCDP composition: map(1)=2.50  parts: 2.00 + 0.50
mixed measures: All output measures must be the same
The second line shows that you cannot mix measures, because the maps of a Laplace count and a Gaussian count return numbers that mean different things. Section 11.7 shows how to bring them to one measure first.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.3 Adaptive composition
Often you choose the second query only after you see the first answer. Composition still holds when each query depends on the earlier answers, if the budget of each is fixed in advance (the full edition’s chapter on composition). The combinator for this is make_adaptive_composition, which needs more arguments, because it cannot read the supporting elements from parts it has not seen.
def adaptive_compositor(d_mids: list[float]) -> dp.Measurement:
    """An adaptive compositor over the toy space: one share of pure-DP budget per query, fixed in advance."""
    return dp.c.make_adaptive_composition(
        input_domain=INT_SPACE[0],
        input_metric=INT_SPACE[1],
        output_measure=dp.max_divergence(),
        d_in=1,  # neighbours add or remove one record
        d_mids=d_mids,  # the epsilon each query may spend, in the order the queries arrive
    )
The argument d_in is the distance between neighbouring datasets, here 1 for one added or removed record. The argument d_mids lists the privacy loss that each query may spend, in order, and the compositor’s privacy map is their sum, here 3.
adaptive: map(1)=3.0
When you invoke the compositor on the data, it releases nothing. It returns a queryable, a small state machine that holds the data and the remaining shares. It accepts a measurement as a query, checks that the measurement’s map at d_in fits within the next share, and answers with the release. The script submits the sum, then the sum again, then the count.
queryable = compositor(data)  # the data go in once; what comes back answers measurements
adaptive_sum = queryable(shortcut)  # spends the first share, 2.0
try:
    queryable(shortcut)  # asks 2.0 of the second share, 1.0
    over_share = "answered"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    over_share = str(err.message)
adaptive_count = queryable(count)  # spends the second share, 1.0
second query over its share: insufficient budget for query: 2.0 > 1.0
third query: out of queries
The shares are spent in order, so the queryable refuses a query larger than the next share, without spending it, and after the second share it refuses every query. A context wraps this object. With split_evenly_over=3 in A first release, the library built an adaptive compositor with three equal shares, the context’s accountant. Each release() submits to the queryable, and the context’s refusal is the “out of queries” above.
On real data, the number of shares sets the noise of every query. The script builds two contexts over the LFS sample, one with the whole budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) on one query and one split evenly over three. Both ask for the sum of HWUSUAL, the hours usually worked per week, without the code 99 for “not applicable” and bounded to 0 to 80 hours. One person has at most 36 rows (the privacy unit), so the sum moves by up to 36 times the upper bound.
LFS context over 1: accountant map(36)=1.0 d_mids=[1.0]
LFS HWUSUAL sum over 1: scale=2,881.04 95% accuracy=8,630.8
LFS context over 3: accountant map(36)=1.0 d_mids=[0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333]
LFS HWUSUAL sum over 3: scale=8,643.11 95% accuracy=25,892.4
true HWUSUAL sum: 56,315,594
Both accountants map the privacy unit’s distance to 1, because the shares add up to the declared budget. But the scale is the sensitivity over the share, so three shares triple the scale and the error bar. An error bar of 26 thousand is small on 56 million hours, but not on a small group. The scale is slightly above the sensitivity over the share because of the float sum’s rounding term (Transformations).

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.4 Odometers
Adaptive composition fixes the budget of each query before the first answer, which is sometimes too early. Fully adaptive composition lets you choose the privacy loss of each query as you go. An odometer tracks the running total of the loss spent, valid at whatever point you stop. The full edition’s chapter on adaptive composition shows why the ordinary theorems fail with adaptively chosen parameters, and which totals are valid. For pure DP the sum of the losses spent is valid, and OpenDP’s odometer reports it.
odometer = dp.c.make_fully_adaptive_composition(
    input_domain=INT_SPACE[0], input_metric=INT_SPACE[1], output_measure=dp.max_divergence()
)
odometer_queryable = odometer(data)
loss_before = odometer_queryable.privacy_loss(1)  # nothing spent yet
odometer_sum = odometer_queryable(shortcut)
loss_after_sum = odometer_queryable.privacy_loss(1)
odometer_count = odometer_queryable(count)
loss_after_count = odometer_queryable.privacy_loss(1)
The constructor takes the three supporting elements of the adaptive compositor, but no d_in and no d_mids. It returns an Odometer, not a Measurement, with no privacy map, because it promises nothing about the total. On the data it gives an odometer queryable, which answers measurements and reports privacy_loss(d_in), the total spent so far at that input distance.
odometer loss: before=0.0 after sum=2.0 after count=3.0 after another count=4.0
odometer loss at d_in=2 after three queries: 8.0
The total starts at zero, grows by the map of each query, and never refuses anything. At distance 2, each Laplace query costs twice as much, so the total doubles. So the odometer says how much you spent, and the decision to spend more is yours. That suits open exploration, but nothing stops the total from passing what you may claim, and the next combinator adds that stop.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.5 Privacy filters
A privacy filter is an odometer with a cap: it refuses any query that would take the running total past a bound fixed in advance. Since the total can never pass the bound, the filter is a measurement with an ordinary privacy map. For pure DP, a cap on the sum of the realized losses is a valid guarantee (the full edition’s chapter on adaptive composition). The combinator make_privacy_filter takes the odometer, the input distance and the cap.
privacy_filter = dp.c.make_privacy_filter(odometer, d_in=1, d_out=2.0)
filter_queryable = privacy_filter(data)
filter_count_1 = filter_queryable(count)
filter_count_2 = filter_queryable(count)
try:
    filter_queryable(count)  # would take the loss to 3.0
    refusal = "answered"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    refusal = str(err.message)
filter: map(1)=2.0
filter third query: filter is now exhausted: pending privacy loss (3.0) would exceed privacy budget (2.0)
filter loss after refusal: filter is exhausted: no more queries can be answered
The filter’s map at distance 1 is the cap, whatever queries arrive later, so the filter is a measurement. Two counts at a cost of 1 each fit under a cap of 2. The filter refuses the third with a message that names the pending total and the budget. After one refusal, the installed version treats the filter as finished, and even privacy_loss raises an error. So read the running total before the query that can exhaust it.
A context wraps a filter when you give it a budget but no split. The script builds a context on the toy data with dp.loss_of(epsilon=2.0) and no split. Its queryable is an odometer queryable behind a filter, and current_privacy_loss reads the odometer. The count query needs an explicit scale, because there is no share to fit.
context without a split: queryable=OdometerQueryable spent=1.0 remaining=1.0

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.6 Chaining and nesting compositors
Compositors and filters are measurements, so you can chain and compose them too. In the first common pattern, a transformation before a compositor does the preprocessing once for all queries. The script chains the clamped sum before an adaptive compositor, so that the queries are measurements on the sum, one integer.
sum_compositor = clamped_sum_only >> dp.c.then_adaptive_composition(
    output_measure=dp.max_divergence(),
    d_in=clamped_sum_only.map(1),  # the sum moves by at most 10 when one record changes
    d_mids=[2.0, 1.0],
)
sum_space = clamped_sum_only.output_domain, clamped_sum_only.output_metric
laplace_on_sum = sum_space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=SUM_SCALE)  # a query on the sum, not on the vector
transformation >> compositor: d_in=10 map(1)=3.0
laplace on the sum: map(10)=2.0
Set d_in with care. The compositor comes after the sum, so its input distance is the sum’s stability map at the privacy unit’s distance, here 10. The then_ form takes the domain and metric from the transformation but cannot know the distance, so compute it with map. A Laplace mechanism of scale 5 on the sum then costs 2, which fits the first share.
In the second pattern, a compositor is inside a compositor. The inner compositor is a measurement whose map is the sum of its shares. So you can submit it to an outer one, which answers with the inner queryable.
outer = adaptive_compositor(d_mids=[3.0, 1.0])
inner = adaptive_compositor(d_mids=[2.0, 1.0])  # a measurement costing 3.0: it fits the outer's first share
outer_queryable = outer(data)
inner_queryable = outer_queryable(inner)  # the answer to a compositor query is a queryable
inner_sum = inner_queryable(shortcut)
outer_count = outer_queryable(count)  # the outer's second share, while the inner queryable stays open
inner_count = inner_queryable(count)  # pure DP composes concurrently, so the inner one still answers
nested: outer map(1)=4.0 inner map(1)=3.0
The outer compositor charges the inner map, 3, whatever the inner one answers later. The script asks the inner queryable for the sum, the outer one for the count, and the inner one again for the count. This works because pure DP supports concurrent composition, where several queryables from one compositor stay open at once. For approximate zCDP and approximate Rényi differential privacy (RDP), post-processing is not proved to hold while an analyst can still interact. So there the library freezes an earlier queryable when a new query arrives. The documentation nests a zCDP compositor inside an approximate-DP one, after it casts the inner measure.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.7 Measure casting
A composition needs all of its parts to have the same output measure. But a Laplace release is measured in pure DP, a Gaussian release in zCDP, and a report usually needs a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) with a slack \(\delta\), the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) of approximate DP. The casting combinators move a measurement from one measure to another, each by a conversion that the full edition derives.
The first conversion goes from pure DP to zCDP. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\) (the full edition’s chapter on concentrated DP), and make_pureDP_to_zCDP applies that to the map. The combinator make_approximate turns a pure-DP measurement into an approximate-DP one with a slack of zero, so that it can compose with measurements that have a real \(\delta\).
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
laplace = space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)
print(dp.c.make_pureDP_to_zCDP(laplace).map(1.0))  # 0.5
print(dp.c.make_approximate(laplace).map(1.0))  # (1.0, 0.0)
You will use the conversion from zCDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) most, because that is how a Gaussian release is reported. A \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism satisfies approximate DP at every slack at once, with a loss that grows as the slack shrinks. So the conversion gives the privacy profile, a curve that gives the smallest privacy loss for each slack. The combinator make_zCDP_to_approxDP returns a measurement whose map is that curve, with the methods epsilon(delta) and delta(epsilon). The script reads it at a slack of one in ten million, for a Gaussian with \(\rho = 0.1\), which is the scale \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\) at unit sensitivity.
gaussian = FLOAT_SPACE >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=math.sqrt(1 / (2 * rho)))  # rho = 1 / (2 scale^2)
profile_measurement = dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(gaussian)
profile = profile_measurement.map(1.0)  # a curve, not a number
epsilon_at_delta = profile.epsilon(delta=delta)
delta_at_one = profile.delta(epsilon=1.0)
fixed = dp.c.make_fix_delta(profile_measurement, delta=delta)  # the curve at one delta: an (epsilon, delta) pair
gaussian: rho=0.1000
profile at rho=0.1: epsilon(delta=1e-07)=2.3484 delta(epsilon=1)=0.008933
simple conversion: 2.6391  improved conversion: 2.3484
fix_delta: map(1.0)=(2.3484, 1e-07)  measure=Approximate(MaxDivergence)
So a budget of \(\rho = 0.1\) is \((2.35, 10^{-7})\)-DP. The third line compares that with the two conversions of the full edition. The simple one is \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho \ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{11.1}\] which gives 2.64 here. The improved conversion of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke minimizes a tighter expression over the Rényi order, and the script’s numerical minimum agrees with OpenDP to four decimals. So OpenDP uses the improved conversion, which matters when you compare its numbers with a paper that quotes the simple one. The full edition’s chapter on RDP conversions shows where the simple formula loses.
A curve cannot compose with a pair, so make_fix_delta evaluates the curve at one \(\delta\) and returns a measurement whose map is the pair. Its output measure is the approximate max divergence, as from make_approximate, so the two can compose. The last casting combinator, make_fixed_approxDP_to_approxDP, turns a fixed pair back into a curve. For a pure-DP release cast with make_approximate, that curve is flat, because \(\varepsilon\)-DP at zero slack holds at every slack.
approximate: map(1.0)=(1.0, 0.0)  measure=Approximate(MaxDivergence)
fixed to profile: epsilon(delta=1e-07)=1.0 epsilon(delta=0)=1.0
laplace count + gaussian count: map(1)=(6.6709, 1e-07)
The last line shows the result. The Laplace count, which Section 11.2 could not compose with the Gaussian count, is cast with make_approximate. The Gaussian count is cast to a curve and fixed at the same slack, and then make_composition accepts the two. The total is large, because a Gaussian count with \(\rho = 0.5\) is expensive at so small a slack: casting makes a composition legal, not cheap. When the Gaussian parts dominate, account the whole release in zCDP and convert once at the end, as the practitioner edition’s release workflow does.

title: 11  Combinators
text:
11.8 Amplification by subsampling
The last combinator changes what a privacy map promises without changing the computation. Suppose that your dataset is a simple random sample of \(n\) people from a population of \(N\), and nobody knows who is in the sample. Then a person may not be in the sample, which makes the release more private with respect to the population. The full edition’s chapter on subsampling derives this amplification and shows why the sampling scheme must match the neighbouring relation. Under pure DP the amplified loss is \[\varepsilon' = \ln\!\Big(1 + \frac{n}{N}\,(e^{\varepsilon} - 1)\Big). \tag{11.2}\] The script prints it next to the library’s map. The combinator make_population_amplification needs a measurement whose input domain has the sample size, because the ratio of the two sizes is part of the guarantee.
def sample_mean() -> dp.Measurement:
    """The Laplace mean of a sample of exactly SAMPLE values in [0, 10]: the domain carries the size."""
    space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0.0, 10.0), nan=False), size=SAMPLE), dp.symmetric_distance()
    return space >> dp.t.then_mean() >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=0.5)


def amplified_mean(population_size: int) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The same mean, with its guarantee read for the population the sample was drawn from."""
    dp.enable_features("honest-but-curious")  # the library cannot check that the data are such a sample
    return dp.c.make_population_amplification(sample_mean(), population_size=population_size)
sample mean: map(2)=2.0000
amplified, population 100: map(2)=0.4940  formula=0.4940
amplified, population 1000: map(2)=0.0619  formula=0.0619
amplifying an unsized domain: elements of the vector domain have unknown size
The maps are read at distance 2, because two datasets of the same size differ by a swap of one record. A swap moves the mean of ten values in a range of 10 by 1, so Laplace noise of half that costs \(\varepsilon = 2\). For a population of a hundred, the release costs about 0.49, and for a thousand, about 0.06, as the formula also gives. The library refuses a vector domain without a size.
The combinator needs the honest-but-curious flag, for the same reason as the Python post-processor: the library cannot verify the claim. The guarantee holds only if the data are a uniform sample of a population of the stated size. It also needs that the readers of the release do not know who is in the sample. So use the map without amplification when the sample depends on the people in it, or when the sampled identities are public.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.1 Types
Every query in this book so far ended with a call such as .laplace() that named no scale, and the context filled the scale in. It used a few utilities that the framework also exposes on their own. Type descriptors say what kind of number a chain carries, a binary search turns a budget into a scale, and a serializer turns a measurement into text. The Context API is a thin layer over these utilities and the combinators of the previous chapter. When you can see the layer, you can predict what a query will do, and rebuild any part of it by hand when the layer refuses.
The chapter ends by taking apart the count query of the first chapter, which gives the same scale of 3. At the end, you can read a type error, run the search a context runs, and store and reload a measurement. You can also say which framework object each line of a Context API program creates.
The script opendp_utilities.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with Polars 1.36.1. Its plain-data queries use the first chapter’s hundred integers from a seeded generator, and its one Polars query counts the rows of the France Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample. The type descriptors, error messages, scales and privacy maps are the same on every run. The released counts change, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so they are in one block marked as one run.
OpenDP’s core is written in Rust, which has signed and unsigned integers from 8 to 128 bits and floats of two widths. The library keeps that precision, because the constants of a privacy proof depend on it. For example, a sum of 32-bit integers can overflow where a 64-bit sum cannot. So every domain, metric and measure carries a type descriptor, such as the T= arguments of the framework chapter. The library never casts one type to another on its own.
You can write a descriptor in three ways, and the snippet shows that they agree. The canonical form is a string such as "i32" or "Vec<f64>". A Python type such as int, float, str or bool is an alias, and list[int] is an alias for a vector. The objects in opendp.typing, such as dp.i32, dp.f64 and dp.Vec[dp.i32], give the same strings with completion in an editor.
The aliases hide one decision: a Python int means a 32-bit integer and a float a 64-bit float, and dp.RuntimeType.infer reads a value’s type in the same way. But NumPy’s default integer has 64 bits, so an integer from an array arrives as i64 and does not meet a domain built with T=int. If all your integers have 64 bits, call set_default_int_type to change what the alias means.
When the types do not meet, the error reads inferred type is XXX, expected YYY, which the documentation’s troubleshooting page lists. The script builds a Laplace mechanism on an integer domain with an integer metric, and then asks for its privacy map at a sensitivity of 1.5.
The message names the type the library inferred from your argument and the type the metric expects, so pass what it expects, here the integer 2. The second pair of lines shows the most common case. The count’s input metric is the symmetric distance, whose distances are unsigned integers, so map(1.0) fails and map(1) succeeds. The documentation names one more cause, a scalar \(\varepsilon\) given to a measure that expects \(\varepsilon\) with the slack \(\delta\) of approximate differential privacy. In 0.16.0 that message is different, as the script prints.
The chapter on limitations and troubleshooting collects the other errors. For this one, read the expected type, then change your argument, your bounds or your data to match it. Do not change the domain to match the argument, because the library chose that type for the proof.

import opendp.prelude as dp

print(dp.atom_domain(T=float))  # AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64)
print(dp.atom_domain((0, 1), T=dp.i32))  # AtomDomain(bounds=[0, 1], T=i32)
print(dp.RuntimeType.parse(list[int]))  # Vec<i32>
print(dp.Vec[dp.i32] == dp.RuntimeType.parse(list[int]))  # True

import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

print(dp.RuntimeType.parse(int))  # i32
print(dp.RuntimeType.infer(np.int64(1)))  # i64
dp.set_default_int_type(dp.i64)
print(dp.RuntimeType.parse(int))  # i64
print(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)))  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=i64))

int_space = dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.absolute_distance(T=int)
laplace_int = int_space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)  # Laplace noise on a 32-bit integer
try:
    laplace_int.map(1.5)  # a float sensitivity, on a metric whose distances are integers
    message = "no error"
except TypeError as err:
    message = first_line(err)

map(2) on an integer metric: 2.0
float d_in on the count: TypeError: inferred type is f64, expected u32
integer d_in on the count: 0.3333

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.2 Parameter search
A measurement has three kinds of parameter. The input distance d_in is the privacy unit’s bound, the output distance d_out is the budget, and the constructor’s own arguments include the noise scale. With all of them fixed, check(d_in, d_out) says whether the measurement is within the budget, as the measurements chapter showed. The answer is monotone: if a scale passes at a budget, every larger scale passes, and so does every larger budget. So the answer changes at one boundary, which a binary search finds, and you can solve for any one parameter from the others.
The library has three forms of the search. The function dp.binary_search takes a predicate on one number and returns the value nearest the boundary on the passing side. The function dp.binary_search_param takes a function that builds a chain from one number, with d_in and d_out, and uses check as the predicate. The function dp.binary_search_chain does the same and returns the chain at the value it found.
import opendp.prelude as dp

print(dp.binary_search(lambda x: x >= 5.0))  # 5.0
print(dp.binary_search(lambda x: x > 5, T=int))  # 6
print(dp.binary_search(lambda x: x <= 5, bounds=(0, None)))  # 5
The three lines show the arguments of a search. Without bounds, the search first finds bounds by steps outwards from zero. The type T says whether the parameter is a float or an integer, and bounds with None on one side give a one-sided search. The script then runs the search of a context on the first chapter’s Laplace mechanism, with a share of \(\varepsilon/3\).
scale = dp.binary_search_param(make_laplace, d_in=1.0, d_out=share)  # the smallest scale within the share
chain = dp.binary_search_chain(make_laplace, d_in=1.0, d_out=share)  # the measurement at that scale
largest_d_in = dp.binary_search(lambda d_in: make_laplace(1.0).check(d_in, EPSILON))  # the other way round
search: scale=3.0000000000000004 chain.map(1.0)=0.3333 chain.check(1.0, share)=True
search: largest d_in at scale 1 within epsilon 1: 1.0
search: gaussian scale for rho=1 at d_in=1: 0.7071
The scale is the smallest one whose map at a sensitivity of 1 is within a third of \(\varepsilon = 1\). It is a little above 3, because the search stops on the passing side of the boundary, and it is the scale that param() reported in the first chapter. The third call asks for the largest sensitivity that a scale of 1 hides within \(\varepsilon = 1\), which is 1. The Gaussian mechanism is measured in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), with a loss \(\rho\) of half the squared sensitivity over the squared scale. So the search for \(\rho = 1\) gives a scale of 0.7071 (the full edition’s chapter on the two mechanisms).
To show what the search does, the script writes it by hand. The predicate is check, the interval starts at 0 to 100, and each step keeps the half that contains the boundary.
def search_by_hand(passes: Callable[[float], bool], low: float, high: float, tolerance: float) -> tuple[float, int]:
    """Bisection on a predicate that fails at `low` and passes at `high`: the smallest passing value, and the steps."""
    steps = 0
    while high - low > tolerance:
        middle = (low + high) / 2
        if passes(middle):
            high = middle  # the boundary is at or below the middle
        else:
            low = middle  # the boundary is above it
        steps += 1
    return high, steps
search by hand: scale=3.000000 after 27 steps
search with bounds (0, 100): 3.0000000000000004
After twenty-seven halvings, the interval of 100 is below a millionth, and its passing end is the scale. The library’s search on the same bounds lands on the float just above 3, so it bisects further than that tolerance. A search can fail in two ways, and the script shows both messages.
search with bounds (0, 1): ValueError: the decision boundary of the predicate is outside the bounds
search on a constant predicate: ValueError: unable to infer bounds
Bounds that do not contain the boundary give the first error, so make them wider. A predicate that never changes gives the second, here one that always passes. With a real chain, it means that no value of the parameter changes the answer, so look at the chain before the bounds.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.3 Serialization
A measurement is a recipe that names its constructors and their arguments. The function dp.serialize writes that recipe as a JSON string, and dp.deserialize turns it back into a measurement. So an analyst can build and inspect a query on a machine without the data, and send the text to the machine that holds them. The script serializes the first chapter’s count measurement.
measurement = count_laplace(3.0)
text = dp.serialize(measurement)  # JSON that names each constructor and its arguments
restored = dp.deserialize(text)
same_space = restored.input_space == measurement.input_space
serialized: 2152 characters, starting {"__function__": "make_chain_mt",
restored: map(1)=0.3333 same input space: True
The text starts with the outermost constructor, the chain of a transformation and a measurement, and nests the rest inside it. The restored measurement has the same input space and privacy map, so a reviewer can check the guarantee before anyone touches the data. The documentation does not promise a stable format between versions, and it asks you not to write it by hand.
Two things do not survive a round trip. The first is the param attribute that a context attaches to a measurement after a search (a later section). It is a Python attribute and not part of the recipe. The second is anything with Python state that the constructors did not set, such as a context, a query or a plugin built from a Python function.
param before a round trip: 3.0000000000000004
param after a round trip: None
serialize a context: OpenDP JSON Encoder does not handle instances of <class 'opendp.context.Context'>
A Polars query has its own route, because Polars can serialize the plan of a LazyFrame to bytes. The method Context.deserialize_polars_plan wraps those bytes in a query on a context of its own. So a client can write the plan against the survey’s schema, and the server can run it on the rows.
client = lfs_context(pl.LazyFrame(schema=frame.collect_schema()))  # the schema, but no rows
plan = client.query().select(dp.len(signed=True)).polars_plan.serialize()  # bytes
server = lfs_context(frame)  # the real data
query = server.deserialize_polars_plan(plan)
summary = query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
plan: 1792 bytes
plan on the server: scale=36.0 95% accuracy=108.3429
The client’s context holds an empty frame with the survey’s schema, and the server’s holds the file. Both must state the budget and the privacy unit of 36 rows per person (the chapter on the data and the context). The plan carries the query but not the guarantee. The scale of 36 is the unit’s distance over the budget, and the error bar is about 108 rows on a count of millions.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.4 The compositor behind a context
The rest of the chapter rebuilds the Context API from the combinators of the previous chapter. The constructor dp.Context.compositor builds an adaptive composition over the data’s space and calls it on the data. That composition takes a list of budgets, the d_mids, and accepts one measurement per share, each of which may depend on the earlier answers. Together they stay within the sum (the full edition’s chapter on composition). The script reads the context’s accountant and builds the same one by hand.
by_hand_accountant = dp.c.make_adaptive_composition(
    input_domain=SPACE[0],
    input_metric=SPACE[1],
    output_measure=dp.max_divergence(),
    d_in=1,  # the privacy unit's distance: one row added or removed
    d_mids=[share] * QUERIES,  # the shares, which add up to the budget
)
queryable = by_hand_accountant(data)  # answers measurement queries on the data, and keeps count
context accountant: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64)) SymmetricDistance() MaxDivergence
context d_in: 1  d_mids: [0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333]
context accountant map(1): 1.0000
by hand accountant map(1): 1.0000  queryable: Queryable(Q=AnyMeasurement)
d_mids by weights [1, 2, 1]: [0.25, 0.5, 0.25]
The context found the domain from the data, a list of floats, and the metric and the measure come from unit_of and loss_of. Both compositions map the unit’s distance to the whole budget, 1. On the data, the accountant returns a queryable, which answers one measurement at a time and refuses when the shares run out. The context keeps that queryable, and the data are only inside it, which is why the first chapter told you to drop your own reference.
The shares come from split_evenly_over or split_by_weights. The context gives the weights to binary_search_param and scales them until the composition’s map at d_in meets the budget. For pure differential privacy, that is the expected proportional split: weights of 1, 2 and 1 give a quarter, a half and a quarter of \(\varepsilon\).

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.5 The query behind a release
The call context.query() returns a Query, which holds a chain and the share it must fit, and on a LazyFrame it is the LazyFrameQuery of the Polars chapters. The chain starts as the data’s space, and each method you call, such as count or laplace, chains on the constructor of that name. So query.count() is space >> dp.t.then_count(). The script shows the type of the chain at each step.
query = plain_query(context)  # the chain is the data's space: a domain and a metric
counted = query.count()  # the chain is a Transformation
noisy = counted.laplace()  # no scale: the chain is a PartialChain, waiting for one number
is_partial = isinstance(noisy._chain, dp.PartialChain)
query chain: tuple -> Transformation -> PartialChain
partial chain: True
resolve a transformation: ValueError: Query is not yet a measurement or odometer.
The important step is laplace() without a scale. The query finds one argument missing from the constructor’s signature, so it wraps the constructor in a partial chain, a function from the missing number to the finished chain. Only one number may be missing at a time, so a second noise step without a scale fails. A query that is still a transformation cannot resolve into a measurement, as the third line shows.
The method resolve finds the number. It calls the partial chain’s fix, which runs binary_search with the predicate “the chain at this value checks within the query’s share”. That is the search of Section 12.2, and fix stores the value on the measurement as param. So param() reports the scale of the search, or None when there was no search.
param of .laplace(): 3.0000000000000004
param of .laplace(scale=3.0): None
two missing parameters: ValueError: gaussian is missing 1 parameter(s).
The script then runs the same search by hand on the same chain, and releases through the queryable built by hand.
by_hand_param = dp.binary_search_param(count_laplace, d_in=1, d_out=share)  # what resolve runs on the chain
by_hand_measurement = count_laplace(by_hand_param)
dp_count_by_hand = queryable(by_hand_measurement)  # what release does: the queryable runs the measurement
resolve: context param=3.0000000000000004 by hand=3.0000000000000004 equal=True
d_mids after context(measurement): [0.3333, 0.3333]
The two scales are equal, because they come from the same search on the same predicate. The method release gives the resolved measurement to the queryable and records the share as spent, so the first share leaves d_mids. The version by hand does the same with queryable(measurement), but nothing records the spend. That record is what the context adds.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.6 Nested compositors and other measures
Two features of the Context API are easier to understand when you can see the chain. The first is Query.compositor, which nests an adaptive composition inside one share. The query’s share becomes the inner budget, split again, and the release of the query returns a new Context and not a number.
inner = plain_query(context).compositor(split_evenly_over=2).release()  # a Context inside one share
inner_scale = plain_query(inner).count().laplace().param()
inner context: d_in=1 d_out=0.3333 d_mids=[0.1667, 0.1667]
inner count scale: 6.0000
outer d_mids after the inner compositor: [0.3333]
The inner context has the outer share, a third of \(\varepsilon\), as its whole budget and splits it in two, so a count inside it gets a scale of 6. The outer context counts the nested compositor as one query, whatever happens inside it, because the composition’s guarantee covers everything its queryable answers.
The second feature is a budget in one measure for a mechanism proved in another. The Laplace mechanism’s measure is the max divergence of pure differential privacy, and the Gaussian mechanism’s is zCDP. When the context’s measure is different, resolve casts the measurement with the converters of Combinators before it checks the budget.
approx = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=data,
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=DELTA),  # approximate differential privacy
    split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
)
laplace_cast = plain_query(approx).count().laplace().resolve()  # pure DP, cast to approximate DP
gaussian_cast = plain_query(approx).count().gaussian().resolve()  # zCDP, converted and its delta fixed
approx share: (0.3333, 3.3e-08)
laplace under (epsilon, delta): Approximate(MaxDivergence) map(1)=(0.3333, 0.0e+00)
gaussian under (epsilon, delta): Approximate(MaxDivergence) map(1)=(0.3333, 3.3e-08)
param after a cast: None
Under an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) budget, make_approximate wraps the Laplace mechanism and reports \((\varepsilon, 0)\), so the search fits only \(\varepsilon\). The Gaussian mechanism goes through make_zCDP_to_approxDP and make_fix_delta, which spend the share’s slack to convert \(\rho\) into \(\varepsilon\). But the cast wraps the old measurement in a new one, so the param attribute is on the inner measurement, and param() reads None. To see the scale, run binary_search_param on the chain yourself.
laplace under rho: ZeroConcentratedDivergence map(1)=0.0333
gaussian under rho: scale=3.8730
gaussian under epsilon: ValueError: Unable to cast measure from ZeroConcentratedDivergence to MaxDivergence
Under a \(\rho\) budget, the Laplace mechanism is cast with make_pureDP_to_zCDP, and the Gaussian mechanism needs no cast, so its param() reports a scale of 3.873. A Gaussian mechanism under a pure \(\varepsilon\) budget cannot be cast, because zCDP never implies pure differential privacy, and the context says so. The full edition’s chapter on concentrated differential privacy derives the conversions behind each cast.
Here are the releases of one run, to read against their error bars.
released (one run):
  survey rows 3811875  (true 3811932, within 108.3 with probability 0.95)
  count by hand 94  (true 100, within 9.4 with probability 0.95)
  count through the context 101  (true 100)
All three are within their bars. The two counts of the hundred integers came from the same measurement, through the queryable built by hand and through the context. So they differ only by their noise.

title: 12  Utilities and the Context API inside
text:
12.7 Summary



Table 12.1: The utilities and the pieces of the Context API, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




"i32", int, dp.i32
Three spellings of one type descriptor
int is i32 and float is f64; NumPy’s integers are i64


dp.set_default_int_type(dp.i64)
Changes what int means for the rest of the program
The clean fix when all your integers have 64 bits


inferred type is XXX, expected YYY
Your argument’s type does not match the metric’s or the domain’s
Change the argument to the expected type, not the domain to the argument


dp.binary_search(predicate, bounds, T)
The value nearest the boundary of a monotone predicate
Pass bounds when the chain is only valid in a range, and T=int for an integer


dp.binary_search_param(make_chain, d_in, d_out)
The smallest scale whose chain checks within the budget
What a context runs for .laplace() without a scale


dp.binary_search_chain(...)
The chain built at the value the search found
It carries no param; use binary_search_param for the number


dp.serialize, dp.deserialize
A measurement as JSON, and back
The recipe survives; param, contexts and Python plugins do not


Context.deserialize_polars_plan(bytes)
A Polars plan from a client, run on the server’s context
The plan carries the query; each context states the guarantee


dp.Context.compositor(...)
An adaptive composition over the data’s space, called on the data
Its queryable holds the data; d_mids are the shares


context.query()
A Query whose chain grows with each constructor
A missing number makes a partial chain; one at a time


query.param()
The scale that resolve found
None when the scale was given or the measure was cast


Query.compositor(...)
A context nested inside one share
The outer context counts it as one query


A Gaussian query under a pure budget
ValueError: Unable to cast measure ...
zCDP never implies pure differential privacy; state the budget with a \(\delta\) or as \(\rho\)

12.8 References

OpenDP documentation: “Typing”, “Parameter Search” and “Serialization” under “Utilities” in the API user guide; “Context” and “API Comparison” in the same guide; and the entry Inferred type is XXX, expected YYY of “Troubleshooting” in Getting Started.
Gaboardi, Hay and Vadhan, “A Programming Framework for OpenDP” (2020): the domains, metrics, measures and maps that the type descriptors and the searches work on.
Dwork, Rothblum and Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy” (2010): composition of adaptively chosen mechanisms, which the compositor behind a context implements.
Bun and Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (2016): zCDP and its conversions to approximate differential privacy, which the measure casts use.
The full edition’s chapters on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, composition and concentrated differential privacy derive the results this chapter states.

title: Extending the library
text:
The framework is open. Anything with a stability map or a privacy map can be a transformation or a measurement, whether OpenDP wrote it or you did. The thread of this part is that a plugin is only as private as its map. So writing one means proving its map, and the library makes the rest safe, from chaining to accounting.
Plugins writes a transformation and a measurement in Python and registers constructors for the Context API. Then it follows the documentation’s two larger examples, a Theil-Sen regression and a private choice of grouping columns. Statistical modelling fits the two models that come with the library, a differentially private linear regression and a differentially private principal component analysis, and reads what each guarantees. Limitations and troubleshooting says what OpenDP does not promise, from floating-point arithmetic to side channels. It also explains the feature flags and the common error messages.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




Plugins
How do I add my own transformation or measurement, and what must I prove about it?


Statistical modelling
How do I fit a private regression or a private principal component analysis with the library’s estimators?


Limitations and troubleshooting
What does the library not guarantee, and what does each common error mean?






At the end of this part you can add a mechanism of your own, fit the built-in models, and say which parts of a deployment stay yours.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.1 Trust and the honest-but-curious flag
Sometimes the mechanism you need is not in the library, such as a new estimator from a paper. The framework of the previous part allows for this, because a transformation is any function with a stability map and a measurement is any function with a privacy map. So you can write both in Python and give them to the library as plugins, which then chain, compose and run through a context like the built-in ones.
The one idea of this chapter is that a plugin is exactly as private as its map, and the library cannot check the map. Every built-in constructor comes with a written proof of its map, but for a plugin that proof is yours. So each example below says why its map is right, or where the documentation leaves that open. You will write a measurement, a transformation and your own spaces, register a constructor for the Context API, and follow the documentation’s Theil-Sen regression and private choice of grouping columns.
The script opendp_plugins.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0. The regression uses the documentation’s toy data, a hundred points on a line with seeded normal noise, and the choice of grouping columns uses the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample. Every map, check, error message, score and candidate range on this page is the same on every run. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the released values appear in one block marked as one run at the end.
The documentation gives two reasons for plugins: the library cannot ship every mechanism, and an idea is easier to try in Python than in Rust. Either way a Python function is at the centre of a guarantee, so the library cannot read it. It cannot tell whether your privacy map is right, whether your function has side effects, or whether it raises an error only on some data.
That is why plugin constructors need a second feature flag next to contrib, named honest-but-curious after its trust model. The author of the plugin is honest, because they have proved their map, and the library guards only against curiosity downstream. Without the flag a plugin constructor refuses to build.
Each constructor’s docstring states the promise. For any two inputs at most d_in apart under the input metric, the output distributions must be at most privacy_map(d_in) apart under the output measure. Also, the function must have no side effects, and the map must be pure. A wrong map breaks the guarantee silently, because the context charges what the map reports. The snippet shows the extreme case, a measurement that returns its input and claims a privacy loss of zero.
The library accepts it, and a context would release the raw data at no charge. The flag records that the claim rests on your word, and the sentence that justifies each map below is what makes that word worth something.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
without the flag: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled

import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance()
leak = dp.m.make_user_measurement(*space, dp.max_divergence(), function=lambda x: x, privacy_map=lambda d: 0.0, TO=list[int])
print(leak.map(1))  # 0.0
print(leak([1, 2, 3]))  # [1, 2, 3]

title: 13  Plugins
13  Plugins
text:
13.3 A transformation plugin
A transformation plugin takes one more argument than a measurement, an output domain. Its map is a stability map, which bounds the distance between two outputs when the inputs are a given distance apart (Transformations). The documentation’s example repeats each record a fixed number of times.
def make_repeat(multiplicity: int) -> dp.Transformation:
    """The documentation's example: a transformation that repeats each record `multiplicity` times."""

    def function(arg: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        return arg * multiplicity

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> int:
        return d_in * multiplicity  # one added record of the input is `multiplicity` added records of the output

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)),
        input_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        output_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)),
        output_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
Both metrics are the symmetric distance, the number of records added or removed. The map multiplies that distance by the multiplicity, because each input record becomes multiplicity output records. The output domain is a second claim. Every output must belong to it, or the function must fail in a way that does not depend on the data. Here it holds, because the output is a vector of integers whenever the input is.
The documentation chains the plugin between built-in steps, a cast from strings and a clamp before a sum, and ends with Laplace noise.
repeat 2: [1, 2] -> [1, 2, 1, 2] map(1)=2 map(3)=6
cast >> repeat 2 >> clamp (1, 2) >> sum: map(1)=4 on ['0', '1', '2', '3'] = 12
... >> laplace scale 1: map(1)=4.0
domain mismatch: DomainMismatch("Intermediate domains don't match
The stability of a chain is the product of the stabilities of its links (Combinators). The cast and the clamp have stability 1 and the repeat has 2. The clamp bounds every value by 2, so one added input record, repeated twice, moves the sum by at most 4. Laplace noise of scale 1 then costs an \(\varepsilon\) of 4. In the last line the cast gives floats, and the library refuses the chain, because it can compare its own spaces.
The library cannot compare the function with the output domain, and that is the second way a transformation plugin goes wrong. The snippet declares that its output lies between 0 and 1 and then returns its input unchanged.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
ints = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int))
bounded = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 1)))
claim = dp.t.make_user_transformation(ints, dp.symmetric_distance(), bounded, dp.symmetric_distance(), function=lambda x: x, stability_map=lambda d: d)
print(claim([5, 6]))  # [5, 6]
print((claim >> dp.t.then_sum()).map(1))  # 1
The sum trusts the bounds and reports a sensitivity of 1, but the real sum moves by the whole value of a record. A wrong output domain becomes a wrong map one step later, so a transformation plugin needs a justification for each.

title: 13  Plugins
section: 13.4 Your own domains, metrics and measures
text:
13.4 Your own domains, metrics and measures
A plugin may work on data that the library has no domain for, such as a data frame, or compare neighbours by a metric that the library does not define. Three constructors let you define your own, and each carries a promise.
A user domain has an identifier and a membership function. The library treats two user domains as equal when their identifiers are equal, and uses that to decide whether two steps chain. So the identifier must name one set only. Otherwise two different domains chain, and the chain’s stability no longer holds. The membership function must return true only for members. A user distance is a metric that is only a name. It promises that your distance is a pseudo-metric, which is zero from a point to itself, never negative, symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality. The snippet declares a domain of even integers and an edit distance on strings, and measures the length of a string.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
even = dp.user_domain("EvenInts", member=lambda x: x % 2 == 0)
print(even.member(4), even.member(3))  # True False
edits = dp.user_distance("EditDistance")
length = dp.t.make_user_transformation(dp.atom_domain(T=str), edits, dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.absolute_distance(T=int), function=len, stability_map=lambda d: d)
print(length("hello"), length.map(1))  # 5 1
print((length >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)).map(1))  # 1.0
The stability map of the length is the identity, because one edit changes the length by at most one. So the chain into Laplace noise closes, and a scale of 1 costs an \(\varepsilon\) of 1 per edit.
A user divergence is a privacy measure of your own. Post-processing must not increase it, because a release must stay private under further computation. The full edition’s chapter on properties proves this for the max divergence. The function new_privacy_profile turns a curve from \(\varepsilon\) to the slack \(\delta\) into a privacy profile that the library can invert. And new_function wraps a Python post-processor, as Combinators did for a bare function after >>. The post-processor must not read global state or raise an error that depends on the data, because either opens a channel from the data that no map accounts for.
import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
renyi = dp.user_divergence("RenyiDivergence(alpha=2)")
rng = np.random.default_rng()
gaussian = dp.m.make_user_measurement(*space, renyi, function=lambda x: float(x + rng.normal()), privacy_map=lambda d: d**2, TO=float)
print(gaussian.map(1.0), gaussian.output_measure)  # 1.0 RenyiDivergence(alpha=2)
try:
    dp.c.make_composition([gaussian, gaussian])
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(str(err).split(". See")[0].strip())  # Type("No match for concrete type ExtrinsicDivergence
profile = dp.new_privacy_profile(lambda eps: 1.0 if eps < 0.5 else 1e-8)
print(profile.delta(epsilon=0.499), profile.epsilon(delta=1e-8))  # 1.0 0.5
double = dp.new_function(lambda x: 2 * x, TO=float)
laplace = space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0)
print((laplace >> double).map(1.0))  # 1.0
The measurement adds standard normal noise. Under the Rényi divergence of order 2 its map is the squared sensitivity. The reason is that this divergence between two unit Gaussians is the squared distance between their centres (the full edition’s chapter on Rényi differential privacy). The composition fails, because the combinators add only the measures that the library defines, so a plugin measure gets map and check and nothing more. The privacy profile answers in both directions, the slack at a given \(\varepsilon\) and the \(\varepsilon\) at a given slack, and its curve must decrease. The post-processor leaves the map of the Laplace measurement unchanged.

title: 13  Plugins
section: 13.5 Registering a constructor for the Context API
text:
13.5 Registering a constructor for the Context API
A plugin built with the framework API is a loose measurement, and A first release showed why every query should go through a context. The function dp.register adds a constructor to the Context API as a method of context.query(). The constructor’s name must start with make_, and the method has the name without that prefix, unless you pass a name. If its first two parameters are input_domain and input_metric, the context fills them in with the output space of the previous step. The documentation calls that partial application, and it gives every built-in make_ constructor its then_ form.
def make_anything_constant(input_domain: dp.Domain, input_metric: dp.Metric, constant: str) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The documentation's constructor for the Context API: it accepts whatever space the previous step outputs."""

    def function(_arg: Any) -> str:
        return constant

    def privacy_map(_d_in: Any) -> float:
        return 0.0

    return dp.m.make_user_measurement(
        input_domain, input_metric, dp.max_divergence(), function=function, privacy_map=privacy_map, TO=str
    )


dp.register(make_anything_constant)  # from now on, context.query().anything_constant(...)
The script builds the documentation’s context over three integers, with a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) split over two queries. Its privacy unit is the book’s 36 contributions per person (the data and the context). Then the script calls the plugin through it.
anything_constant: map(36)=0.0 release=denied
budget spent by the plugin query: [0.5]
clamp >> sum >> int_constant: release=denied
register twice: 'anything_constant' is already registered in the Context API. Please choose a different name.
register without make_: constructor.__name__ must start with 'make_', found select_cols
On the second line the map of the plugin is zero, but the context charged the query its full share. The reason is that a context splits the budget before it sees a query (Utilities and the Context API inside). So a cheap plugin does not give the difference back.
The third line uses the documentation’s other style, make_int_constant, without the two leading parameters. Its input space is fixed to integers, so it works only after a clamp and a sum. The documentation recommends the first style, but a constructor that accepts any space should check that the space suits its function. The last two lines are the errors of register for a name already taken and for a name without the prefix.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.6 A Theil-Sen regression
The documentation’s first larger example fits a line through noisy points. Least squares is a poor private estimator, because one far-away point can move the line by any amount. The Theil-Sen estimator takes the median of the slopes through pairs of points instead, and OpenDP already releases medians privately. The documentation’s variant pairs the points at random and fits a line through each pair. It records where each line crosses two vertical cuts, at a quarter and three quarters of the range of \(x\), and the medians at the cuts are two points on the fitted line. The library ships a vetted version of this estimator (Statistical modelling), so this one is for learning how plugins, your own transformations and measurements, combine.
The first plugin is the pairing, a transformation from a two-column array to a two-column array of predictions.
def pairwise_predict(data: NDArray[np.float64], x_cuts: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
    """Pair the rows at random, fit a line through each pair, and predict y at the two cut points."""
    data = np.array(data, copy=True)[: len(data) // 2 * 2]
    np.random.shuffle(data)
    p1, p2 = np.array_split(data, 2)
    dx, dy = (p2 - p1).T
    x_bar, y_bar = (p1 + p2).T / 2
    points = dy / dx * (x_cuts[None].T - x_bar) + y_bar
    return points.T[dx != 0]
The transformation wraps that function.
def make_pairwise_predict(x_cuts: NDArray[np.float64], runs: int = 1) -> dp.Transformation:
    """A transformation from the (x, y) rows to the predictions: one row per pair and run."""

    def function(arg: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
        return np.vstack([pairwise_predict(arg, x_cuts) for _ in range(runs)])

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> int:
        return d_in * runs  # each record sits in one pair, so it changes one prediction per run

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float),
        input_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        output_domain=dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float),
        output_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
The domains, from the library’s NumPy extension, are arrays with two columns. The documentation states the map, the input distance times the number of runs, without its argument: each record sits in one pair, so it changes at most one prediction per run. That claim is weaker than a built-in map in two ways. The pairing is random, so the claim is about a coupling of two runs, not about a function. And the function drops the last record when the count is odd, so removing one record can change the pair of another. That is the kind of gap the flag asks you to notice.
The second plugin selects one column of the predictions, and the library’s quantile does the rest.
def make_select_column(j: int) -> dp.Transformation:
    """Column j of the predictions as a vector; one row in is one row out, so the stability is the input distance."""

    def function(arg: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
        return arg[:, j]

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> int:
        return d_in

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float),
        input_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        output_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float)),
        output_metric=dp.symmetric_distance(),
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
The library’s quantile then runs once for each cut.
def make_private_medians(output_measure: dp.Measure, y_bounds: tuple[float, float], scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """The private median of the predictions at each cut, by the library's quantile, composed."""
    median = dp.m.then_private_quantile(output_measure, candidates=np.linspace(*y_bounds, 100), alpha=0.5, scale=scale)
    return dp.c.make_composition(
        [
            make_select_column(0) >> dp.t.then_drop_null() >> median,
            make_select_column(1) >> dp.t.then_drop_null() >> median,
        ]
    )
Selecting a column keeps one row per row, so its stability is the input distance. The private quantile scores a hundred candidates between the public bounds of \(y\) and picks one by noisy max (Measurements), at a cost of the input distance over the scale. The composition adds the two costs (the full edition’s chapter on composition). Solving for the line is post-processing of two released numbers and costs nothing.
def make_private_theil_sen(
    output_measure: dp.Measure, x_bounds: tuple[float, float], y_bounds: tuple[float, float], scale: float
) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Pair and predict, release the two medians, then solve for the slope and the intercept (post-processing)."""
    x_cuts = x_bounds[0] + (x_bounds[1] - x_bounds[0]) * np.array([0.25, 0.75])
    p_inv = np.linalg.inv(np.vstack([x_cuts, np.ones_like(x_cuts)]).T)  # the line through two points

    def to_coefficients(medians: list[float]) -> tuple[float, float]:
        slope, intercept = p_inv @ np.array(medians)
        return float(slope), float(intercept)

    return make_pairwise_predict(x_cuts) >> make_private_medians(output_measure, y_bounds, scale) >> to_coefficients
The script runs it with the documentation’s bounds and a scale of 1, on the toy points. Their true line has slope 2 and intercept 1.
theil-sen: x cuts -1.5 and 1.5, 100 candidates from -10.0 to 10.0 step 0.2020
pairwise predict: map(1)=1 medians: map(1)=2.0 theil-sen: map(1)=2.0 map(2)=4.0
toy data: n=100 least-squares slope=2.0573 intercept=1.0376
pairs: 50 medians at the cuts -2.2424 and 4.2857
selection bound: 26.2 score units at noise scale 2.0
cut -1.5: best candidate -2.3232 score 2; within the bound: -2.9293 to -1.5152 (8 candidates)
cut 1.5: best candidate 4.3434 score 8; within the bound: 3.3333 to 6.3636 (16 candidates)
The pairing has stability 1 and the two medians cost 2 together, so the estimator costs an \(\varepsilon\) of 2 per record. The exact medians of the fifty pairwise predictions are the values that the private medians aim at.
The last three lines give the bound for the released medians. The private quantile adds exponential noise of scale 2 to each score and picks the best. The difference of two such draws is a Laplace draw, so the chance that a worse candidate wins falls exponentially in its gap to the best. A union bound over the other 99 candidates gives the printed bound, which a losing candidate beats at most once in ten thousand runs.

title: 13  Plugins
text:
13.7 Choosing grouping columns privately
The documentation’s second larger example solves a problem that comes before any grouped release. You want to choose grouping columns without looking at the data. Some columns are too uniform and others too diverse, and too many columns leave most groups too small to pass the thresholds of Grouping. So the example scores each candidate set by how many of its groups reach a public minimum of rows. Then it picks a set with the exponential mechanism, which chooses a candidate with a probability that grows exponentially in its score (the full edition’s chapter on selection).
The score is a transformation plugin on a user domain, because the library has no domain for a whole data frame. The documentation scores a pandas frame, and the same score runs here on a Polars frame.
def score(frame: pl.DataFrame, columns: tuple[str, ...], min_rows: int) -> float:
    """How many groups of these columns have at least `min_rows` rows."""
    return float(frame.group_by(list(columns)).len().filter(pl.col("len") >= min_rows).height)
The transformation applies it to every candidate set.
def make_grouping_cols_score(
    input_domain: dp.Domain, input_metric: dp.Metric, candidates: list[tuple[str, ...]], min_rows: int
) -> dp.Transformation:
    """A transformation from the frame to one score per candidate set of grouping columns."""
    dp.assert_features("contrib")

    def function(frame: pl.DataFrame) -> list[float]:
        return [score(frame, columns, min_rows) for columns in candidates]

    def stability_map(d_in: int) -> float:
        return float(d_in)  # one row changes one group's size, so it moves each score by at most 1

    return dp.t.make_user_transformation(
        input_domain=input_domain,
        input_metric=input_metric,
        output_domain=dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)),
        output_metric=dp.linf_distance(T=float),  # not monotonic: a person's rows may be added and removed
        function=function,
        stability_map=stability_map,
    )
The output metric is the L-infinity distance, the largest change in any one score, because noisy max compares scores. The map is the identity, because one row belongs to one group of each candidate, so it moves each score by at most one.
The documentation declares the metric monotonic, which halves the cost of noisy max. That is right when neighbours differ by one row added or one row removed, because every score then moves the same way. Here a person has up to 36 rows, and a neighbouring dataset can add some and remove others, so the scores can move both ways. So the script keeps the metric plain and pays the factor of two (the full edition’s chapter on sensitivity).
The measurement chains the scores into noisy max and names the chosen candidate, and it is registered so that a context can run it.
def make_select_grouping_cols(
    input_domain: dp.Domain, input_metric: dp.Metric, candidates: list[tuple[str, ...]], min_rows: int, scale: float
) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Score the candidates, pick one by the exponential mechanism, and name its columns."""

    def name(index: int) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return candidates[index]  # post-processing: the index is already private

    scores = make_grouping_cols_score(input_domain, input_metric, candidates, min_rows)
    return scores >> dp.m.then_noisy_max(dp.max_divergence(), scale) >> name


dp.register(make_select_grouping_cols)


def frame_domain() -> dp.Domain:
    """A domain for a Polars DataFrame: the library has none, so membership is a Python check."""

    def member(value: object) -> bool:
        return isinstance(value, pl.DataFrame)

    return dp.user_domain("PolarsDataFrameDomain", member=member)
On the survey the candidates are every non-empty subset of six columns. Five are SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER and AGE, in seven bands, and the sixth is the person identifier PIDENT. A group counts in a score when it has at least 100 rows, a public choice. The context is built over the collected frame, with the user domain passed as domain, the privacy unit of 36 contributions and a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\). The script leaves out the scale, so that the context searches for one against the map of the plugin.
LFS: 3,811,932 rows; candidate columns SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE, PIDENT; 63 candidate sets
distinct values: SEX 2 ILOSTAT 4 YEAR 9 QUARTER 4 AGE 7 PIDENT 1,682,306
score: groups of at least 100 rows
rank 1: SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE score 996 of 1,105 groups
rank 2: ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE score 504 of 570 groups
rank 3: SEX, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE score 432 of 470 groups
sets with PIDENT: 32, largest score 0
select scale 72: map(36)=1.0 monotonic would be 0.5
context query: param scale=72.0
within 910 of the best: 10 candidates
The scores, computed at development time on this public survey, have the shape the documentation describes. The five columns without the identifier score best, and the next set scores about half of that. Every set with PIDENT scores zero, because no person has a hundred rows. The map is twice the sensitivity over the scale, so the search finds a scale of 72 for an \(\varepsilon\) of 1.
By the argument used for the medians, a set that scores more than 910 below the best wins at most once in ten thousand runs. Ten sets are within that bound. The best beats the runner-up by 492, under seven noise scales, so it wins most runs, but any of the ten can appear. That spread is the price of the person-level unit, because a person can move each score by 36 while the scores are only in the hundreds. A higher minimum group size lowers every score and makes the choice more random. A larger budget is the only other lever.
released (one run):
  python laplace of 10.0: 9.6979  (within 6.0 with probability 0.95)
  repeated sum of ['0', '1', '2', '3'] with laplace scale 1: 13  (true 12)
  theil-sen: slope 2.1549 intercept 1.1111  (medians at the cuts -2.1212 and 4.3434)
  grouping columns: SEX, ILOSTAT, YEAR, QUARTER, AGE
The Python Laplace landed within its error bar, and the repeated sum within one of the truth. Both private medians fell inside their candidate ranges, so the slope and the intercept are near 2 and 1, and the chosen columns are the five that score best. Your run can differ in each of these.
