title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.1 A model or a table?
Every release so far has been a table of statistics, such as a count, a sum, a mean or a quantile per group. Often the question is about a relation instead, such as how many hours people actually work for each hour they usually work, or which directions of a table carry its variance. OpenDP ships two models for such questions, a differentially private linear regression and a differentially private principal component analysis (PCA), both with interfaces like those of scikit-learn. The one idea of this chapter is that a fitted model is a release like any other. Its cost is the privacy map of the measurement behind fit, not the argument named epsilon.
You will fit the regression on the documentation’s generated points and on the Labour Force Survey (LFS), read its privacy loss, and see why its sensitivity is bounded. You will fit the PCA on the documentation’s generated table and compare it with NumPy’s exact decomposition. Then you will meet the NumPy domain under both estimators, and the questions a reviewer should ask about a private model.
The script opendp_statistical_modelling.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with scikit-learn 1.8.0. A seeded NumPy generator makes the toy data and fixes how the regression pairs its rows. So the exact fits, the bounds, the cut points and every privacy map are the same on every run. The released fits change, because OpenDP’s generator cannot be seeded, and they appear in one block marked as one run.
The documentation’s page on statistical modelling makes one point before any code. When you know which relation you need, a model made for it spends the whole budget on the few numbers that answer the question. A slope costs two private medians, as the next section shows, while a table fine enough to read the slope from would cost a noisy count in every cell. In the same way, the PCA releases a few directions, not a full covariance matrix.
The flexible alternative is synthetic data, which answers any later question and can go to people who need microdata. The price is accuracy, because a copy that serves every question answers each one less accurately than a direct release under the same budget (AIM and MST). So release a table when the questions are counts, a model when the question is a relation, and synthetic data when the questions are not yet known.
The two models are narrow on purpose. The regression takes one explanatory column and one response, and the PCA takes a numeric table whose rows have a bounded length. For many explanatory variables, use the methods of the full edition’s chapter on private empirical risk minimization, which OpenDP does not ship.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.2 Linear regression
A least-squares line is a poor thing to release directly. Its slope is a ratio of sums whose sensitivity is unbounded unless you clip both columns, and clipping changes the line. OpenDP ships a Theil-Sen regression, which uses medians instead. It pairs the rows at random, fits the line through each pair, and reads each line at two fixed cut points on the x axis. At each cut point it releases the median of those readings with a private quantile. Then it solves the two medians for a slope and an intercept, which is post-processing and costs nothing.
The sensitivity is bounded because of how the private median chooses. It scores every candidate on a fixed grid by how many readings lie on either side of it. Then the exponential mechanism picks a candidate with a probability that favours high scores. One person’s row sits in one pair, so it moves one reading and changes the score of any candidate by at most one. How far the reading moved does not matter, so the estimator needs no clipping and survives a person who reports a thousand hours. The full edition’s chapter on selection derives the exponential mechanism and the private quantile, and its chapter on sensitivity explains why a count of readings is the quantity to bound.
def make_regression(
    x_bounds: tuple[float, float], y_bounds: tuple[float, float], scale: float, runs: int = 1
) -> dp.sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression:
    """The private Theil-Sen regression under pure differential privacy, with public bounds on x and y."""
    return dp.sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression(
        dp.max_divergence(),  # the output measure: the privacy loss is read in epsilon
        x_bounds=[x_bounds],  # fixes the two cut points, a quarter and three quarters of the way across
        y_bounds=y_bounds,  # the range over which the candidate medians are spread
        scale=scale,  # the noise scale of each of the two private medians
        runs=runs,  # how many random pairings to pool; each multiplies the privacy loss
    )
The first argument is the output measure, and dp.max_divergence() asks for pure differential privacy (DP), whose parameter is the privacy loss \(\varepsilon\). The bounds are public and never clip the data. The x bounds only place the two cut points, at the fractions fraction_bounds of the way across, a quarter and three quarters by default. The y bounds only fix the grid of candidates_count evenly spaced candidates for each median, a hundred by default. The scale is the noise scale of each private median, and runs repeats the random pairing and pools the readings. Plugins builds the same estimator from plugins, as the documentation does.
regression space: NPArray2Domain(num_columns=2, nan=True, T=f64) SymmetricDistance() MaxDivergence
regression map: scale=1 runs=1 -> epsilon=2.0
regression map: scale=2 runs=1 -> epsilon=1.0
regression map: scale=2 runs=3 -> epsilon=3.0
The measurement attribute of the estimator reads like any other measurement. Its input is a two-column NumPy array under the symmetric distance, so its map at distance 1 is the privacy loss for adding or removing one row. Two medians at scale 1 cost \(\varepsilon = 2\), and doubling the scale halves that. Three runs at scale 2 cost \(\varepsilon = 3\), because a row then sits in three pairs and moves three readings. More runs make the median better defined, but at a fixed budget they force a larger scale, so they rarely pay on a large dataset.
The documentation’s toy data is a hundred points with a true slope of 2 and an intercept of 1, here from a seeded generator. The script prints the exact values to read a fit against.
toy: n=100 cut points=[-1.5, 1.5] candidate step=0.2020
toy least squares: slope=2.0275 intercept=0.9725
toy median line, no noise: slope=2.0379 intercept=1.0786 readings=50
The candidate step is the y range divided into 99 intervals, about 0.2. The cut points are 3 apart, so one grid step at one median changes the slope by about 0.07, before any noise. The median line is what the estimator would return with exact medians and the seeded pairing, from the 50 readings of 100 points. It is close to least squares because the noise in the toy data is symmetric.

14.2.1 Actual hours against usual hours on the survey
The survey question is how many hours people actually worked in the reference week for each hour they usually work. The script takes the people at work in the fourth quarter of 2013 with both hours recorded. The survey codes hours from 0 to 98, so the bounds are public, and it drops the code 99, “not applicable”. It also keeps the first row of each person, so that the privacy unit of the fit is one person (Identifier truncation). These steps run in Polars before the array reaches the measurement, so they are your claim and not the library’s.
survey: working people in 2013 Q4 with hours recorded: 36,914 (one row each)
survey: of them with 0 actual hours that week: 4,109
survey: bounds=(0.0, 98.0) cut points=[24.5, 73.5] candidate step=0.9899
survey least squares: slope=0.8582 intercept=-0.1935
survey median line, no noise: slope=1.0000 intercept=0.0000 medians=[24.50, 73.50]
survey readings: 16,463 pairs; within one candidate step of the medians: 5,606 and 5,252
The two exact fits disagree, and that is the lesson. Of the 36,914 people, 4,109 worked no hours that week, through leave or illness, and they pull least squares down to 0.86 actual hours per usual hour. The median line ignores them, because most pairs of people lie on the line where actual equals usual. So its medians are the cut points themselves, and its slope is exactly 1. A private Theil-Sen fit therefore estimates the typical relation, not the average one, and the median line is the exact value to compare it with. The readings are fewer than half the people, because a pair with equal usual hours has no slope, and thousands of them lie within one grid step of each median.
model = make_regression(HOURS_BOUNDS, HOURS_BOUNDS, scale=REGRESSION_SCALE)
epsilon = model.measurement.map(1)  # the privacy loss for adding or removing one person's row
survey_slope, survey_intercept = fit_regression(model, hours, seed)
survey private fit: scale=2 epsilon=1.0
The fit at scale 2 costs \(\varepsilon = 1\) for one person. Like scikit-learn, fit takes the explanatory column as a two-dimensional array and the response as a vector. It returns a fitted scikit-learn LinearRegression, so coef_, intercept_ and predict work as usual.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.3 Principal component analysis
A PCA finds the directions along which a table varies most. OpenDP’s version releases three things under one budget. They are the mean of the rows, the singular values, which say how much variance each direction carries, and the components, which are the directions.
The algorithm, from Amin and others (2019), scales every row into a ball of radius row_norm and centres the rows on a private mean. Then it forms the matrix of sums of squares and cross-products. It releases the eigenvalues of that matrix with Laplace noise, because replacing one row moves their sum by at most twice the squared row norm. Then it draws the eigenvectors one at a time with the exponential mechanism on the sphere, which favours directions of high variance, and removes each drawn direction from the matrix.
So two facts must be public. The row norm is the sensitivity of the whole algorithm, and every map below is in units of it. The number of rows is part of the domain, which gives the mean a known divisor. So neighbouring tables have the same size with one row replaced, which is distance 2 under the symmetric distance. The library declares both facts and does not check them, as the reviewer’s section shows. The budget is split in three equal parts for the mean, the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, and the third for the eigenvectors is split again over the draws.
The table is the documentation’s, ten thousand centred rows of four columns from a normal distribution with a random covariance. A seeded generator makes the exact decomposition reproducible.
pca table: 10,000 rows x 4 columns, row length mean=8.53 max=36.56
pca table: rows longer than 1: 99.9%  longer than 40: 0.0%
pca exact, raw rows: singular values=[901.9, 278.6, 222.2, 156.9]
pca exact, rows clamped to 1: singular values=[80.48, 40.67, 34.29, 26.29]
pca exact, rows clamped to 1: first component=[-0.614, -0.534, -0.526, -0.247]
The documentation fits with row_norm=1.0, and the first two lines show what that means here. Almost every row is longer than 1, so the clamp scales almost every row onto the unit sphere. The algorithm can then only estimate the singular values of the clamped table, about 80 instead of about 900 for the first. The directions survive the clamp, because scaling a row does not turn it, so the release is compared with the first component of the clamped table. The script also fits with a row norm of 40, which clamps nothing, to show the other side of the trade.
def make_pca(epsilon: float, row_norm: float, n_components: int | None = None) -> dp.sklearn.decomposition.PCA:
    """The private PCA of the generated table, with the two public facts the algorithm needs."""
    return dp.sklearn.decomposition.PCA(
        epsilon=epsilon,
        row_norm=row_norm,  # public: every row is scaled into a ball of this radius before anything else
        n_samples=PCA_ROWS,  # public: the exact number of rows, which fixes the domain
        n_features=PCA_COLUMNS,
        n_components=n_components,  # None releases every component
    )
pca = make_pca(PCA_EPSILON, ROW_NORM)
measurement = pca.measurement()  # the measurement behind fit(), for its map and for compositors
pca.fit(table)  # the private release: the mean, the singular values and the components
pca model: PCA(epsilon=1.0, n_components=4, n_features=4, n_samples=10000, row_norm=1.0)
pca space: NPArray2Domain(size=10000, num_columns=4, nan=True, T=f64) SymmetricDistance() MaxDivergence
pca map: map(2)=2.0 map(1)=2.0 check(2, 1.0)=False check(2, 2.0)=True
make_private_pca unit_epsilon=1: map(2)=1.0 map(1)=1.0
pca n_components=2: map(2)=2.0
pca composition of epsilon 1 and 0.5: map(2)=3.0
Read the third line twice. The model was built with epsilon=1.0, but the map of its measurement at distance 2, one replaced row, is 2.0. And check confirms that this fit does not stay within \(\varepsilon = 1\).
The reason is in the constructor. The PCA class calls the framework’s make_private_pca with twice its epsilon, divided by n_changes, the number of rows one person may change. The fourth line shows that make_private_pca with a unit budget of 1 has a map of 1.0 at distance 2. So in version 0.16.0 a PCA(epsilon=1.0) fit costs \(\varepsilon = 2\) per changed row by its own map, and the map is what you should quote. The map is flat below distance 2, because the algorithm is an adaptive composition declared at that distance (Combinators).
The fifth line shows that two components leave the total unchanged, and only the split inside changes. The library draws one eigenvector fewer than there are columns, because the others fix the last direction. So the third for the eigenvectors is split over three draws for four components and over two draws for two, and each draw gets more. The measurement() method is there for the compositors. The last line composes a fit at epsilon=1.0 with one at epsilon=0.5, and the maps add to 3.0 at distance 2.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.4 The NumPy domain underneath
Both estimators use dp.numpy.array2_domain, the domain of two-dimensional NumPy arrays, described by a number of columns, an optional number of rows and the element type. It can also have a norm, its order p and an origin, which say that every row lies within that norm of the origin. A domain with a norm is a promise about the data, and make_np_clamp is the transformation that makes the promise true.
import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
rows = dp.numpy.array2_domain(num_columns=2, T=float)
clamp = dp.numpy.make_np_clamp(rows, dp.symmetric_distance(), norm=1.0, p=2, origin=np.array([1.0, 2.0]))
print(clamp(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [4.0, 6.0], [1.5, 2.0]])).tolist())  # [[1.0, 2.0], [1.6, 2.8], [1.5, 2.0]]
print(clamp.map(1))  # 1
print(clamp.output_domain)  # NPArray2Domain(origin=[1. 2.], norm=1.0, p=2, num_columns=2, nan=False, T=f64)
The clamp leaves the first and third rows alone, because they lie within distance 1 of the origin, and pulls the second row from distance 5 back to the sphere. Its stability map is the identity, because clamping each row on its own neither adds nor removes rows (Transformations). Its output domain records the norm, the order, the origin, and that no value is missing.
That output domain is what make_private_pca prefers to receive. Such a domain states that the rows are already bounded around a known centre. So the algorithm skips the private mean and its third of the budget.
bounded domain: NPArray2Domain(origin=[0. 0. 0. 0.], norm=1.0, p=2, size=10000, num_columns=4, nan=True, T=f64)
pca on the bounded domain: map(1)=0.50 map(2)=1.00 map(4)=2.00
The script passes an explicit split as a PCAEpsilons, with half for the eigenvalues, a sixth for each of three eigenvectors and nothing for the mean. The map is then linear in the distance, not flat, because no compositor is declared in between. Use this route when the centre is public, for example for scores on a known scale, and the class when it is not.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.5 What a reviewer should ask
The first question is the privacy unit. Both estimators count rows, so the claim “one person” holds only if each person has one row, which on the survey was your own Polars step. The second is the bounds. The bounds of the regression and the row norm and row count of the PCA must come from the code book or the domain. A bound read from the data leaks it. The third is which features are on, because a feature is a statement about what you accept on trust.
regression without honest-but-curious: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled
pca without honest-but-curious: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled
pca without idealized-numerics: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "idealized-numerics", but not enabled
regression without idealized-numerics: constructed
pca with n_samples one short of the table: fitted without complaint
Both estimators need honest-but-curious, because they use user-defined transformations whose functions and stability maps the library takes as written. For example, the pairing step of the regression claims that one row moves runs readings, and the library records that claim without proof. The PCA also needs idealized-numerics, which concedes that its proofs hold for real arithmetic and not for floating point. Every guarantee of the PCA rests on that concession, and the library’s own source notes that it knows no floating-point-safe sampler for the eigenvector draw. The regression constructs without the flag, because its private medians run in the Rust core and only the pairing is Python.
The last line is the trap for a reviewer. The number of rows is part of the domain of the PCA, but the library does not check that the array has that many rows. So a wrong n_samples is a wrong guarantee that nothing reports. The clamp enforces the row norm, and the bounds of the regression need no enforcement because its sensitivity does not depend on them. Limitations and troubleshooting collects the other things the library does not check.

title: 14  Statistical modelling
text:
14.6 The releases of one run
released (one run):
  toy private fit: slope=1.9529 intercept=1.0101
  survey private fit: slope=1.0101 intercept=-0.9899
  survey private fit at 35 usual hours: 34.36 actual
  pca row_norm=1: singular values=[80.48, 40.66, 34.28, 26.37]
  pca row_norm=1: |cos| with exact components=[1.000, 0.998, 0.996, 0.996]
  pca row_norm=1: mean=[0.001, 0.002, 0.001, 0.001]  explained variance ratio=[0.648, 0.165, 0.117, 0.070]
  pca row_norm=40: singular values=[906.8, 268.6, 212.6, 153.2] (exact [901.9, 278.6, 222.2, 156.9])
  pca row_norm=40: |cos| with exact components=[0.996, 0.659, 0.426, 0.086]
  pca n_components=2: returned the model: True  singular values=[80.41, 40.64]
  pca n_components=2: |cos| with exact components=[0.999, 0.999]
The toy fit is about one grid step off the least-squares line at one cut point, which is what a private median on 50 readings at \(\varepsilon = 2\) gives. The test allows the slope within 0.3 of the least-squares slope and the intercept within 0.5, about three grid steps at either cut point. A candidate three steps from the best scores lower by every reading in between, and the exponential mechanism makes such a candidate rare at this budget.
The survey fit is the same on every run. The medians sit exactly at the cut points, and the nearest candidates on the grid give a slope of 1.0101 and an intercept of about \(-1\). Thousands of readings lie within one grid step of each median, so the next candidate scores thousands worse than the best, and noise at scale 2 never overturns that gap. The error of the fit is therefore the grid, not the noise, and a finer candidates_count removes it at no cost in privacy. The test allows the slope within 0.1 of the median line and the intercept within 4 hours, two grid steps at the lower cut point. The fit predicts about 34.4 actual hours for someone who usually works 35.
At row norm 1 the PCA recovers the singular values of the clamped table to within a tenth, and all four directions to a cosine above 0.99. Its mean is within a few thousandths of the true zero. The test allows each singular value within 1 and each cosine above 0.9. Both bounds leave a wide margin, because the Laplace noise on the eigenvalues is a few units against eigenvalues in the thousands, and the four directions are well separated.
At row norm 40 the singular values are those of the raw table, within a few percent, but only the first direction is right. The concentration of the eigenvector sampler falls with the square of the row norm, so the last three directions are close to random. The test checks only the first singular value, within 30, and the first cosine, above 0.9. The two-component fit returns the model itself, and its two directions are as good as the first two of the four-component fit.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.1 What OpenDP does not promise
Every chapter so far has shown what OpenDP guarantees, and this one shows where the guarantee stops. The one idea is that the guarantee covers exactly what passes through a measurement with a checked proof. The rest is yours to account for, such as the arithmetic that the proof assumes, the code before the context, and channels other than the output. Most refusals of the library keep you on the right side of that line, so an error message is usually the guarantee doing its job.
The chapter follows the documentation’s pages on limitations, on features and on troubleshooting. You will read what the library does not promise, see what each feature flag gates, and mark out what lies outside the guarantee. Then you will meet the error messages of the earlier chapters again, each with its cause and its fix, and see what a reviewer checks before trusting a release.
The script opendp_limitations.py reproduces every message on this page with OpenDP 0.16.0 and Polars 1.36.1. It uses tiny lists for the framework calls and the France Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample behind a context for the Polars ones. The messages, the sensitivities, the scales and the error bar are the same on every run. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the one released count changes, and it appears at the end in a block marked as one run.
The documentation’s page on limitations names five things, and each changes how you deploy the library. The first is arithmetic. A privacy proof is about real numbers, but a computer adds floating-point numbers, which round. Casacuberta, Shoemate, Vadhan and Wagaman (2022) found that several libraries computed the sensitivity of a sum as if the arithmetic were exact. The rounding made the true sensitivity larger, so the noise was too small and the stated \(\varepsilon\) was wrong.
OpenDP puts the rounding into the proof. To see this, the script builds a float sum and an integer sum of values between 0 and 80 (Transformations). Then it asks each for its sensitivity when 36 rows are added or removed.
In exact arithmetic both would be 36 times 80. The map of the float sum adds a small term for the rounding error, and the integer sum needs none, because integers add exactly. The term grows with the number of rows, so a float sum on the LFS needs a public bound on that number (Essential statistics). The library puts any component that still assumes exact arithmetic behind the idealized-numerics flag. So prefer integer statistics where you can, and otherwise read the scale of a float statistic from the library, not from the formula.
The second limitation is side channels. OpenDP is not hardened against them, so the time, the memory and the cache lines of a query may depend on the data. No proof covers what an attacker learns from them. So the deployment question is who can interact with the running system. An analyst who submits queries through a queue is in a different position from one with a shell on the machine. Keep the second kind out, or accept that the guarantee is weaker than the \(\varepsilon\) you record.
The third is vetting. Every component of OpenDP is meant to come with a written proof and a review of that proof, and until the review is finished the component needs the contrib flag. The documentation expects the review to find bugs in code and in proofs. So every release in this book rests on proofs that no second reader has checked yet. Record which components a release used, so that you can revisit it if one is corrected.
The fourth is stability. Until version 1.0.0, OpenDP’s interfaces may change between minor releases. So pin the version, as this book pins 0.16.0. Keep a test that reruns your release code, so that a changed default fails the test before it changes a number. The fifth is software quality, because no deployment can rule out an unknown bug. So keep a record of the run from which you can compute the guarantee again, as Release and governance in the practitioner edition describes.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
def sum_sensitivities(d_in: int) -> tuple[float, int]:
    """The sensitivity of a float sum and of an integer sum of values in [0, 80], at `d_in` added or removed rows."""
    float_sum = (dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=HOURS_BOUNDS)), dp.symmetric_distance()) >> dp.t.then_sum()
    int_sum = (dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 80))), dp.symmetric_distance()) >> dp.t.then_sum()
    return float_sum.map(d_in), int_sum.map(d_in)
float sum of 36 rows in [0, 80]: sensitivity 2880.0000007451
int sum of 36 rows in [0, 80]: sensitivity 2880

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.2 The feature flags
The feature flags are how the library asks for your consent to each of those limitations. There are four, plus a deprecated alias, and all are off until you call dp.enable_features. A first release switched contrib on without showing what happens otherwise, so the script switches it off, tries the Laplace mechanism of that chapter, and switches it back on.
dp.disable_features("contrib")
without_contrib = refusal(lambda: space >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=1.0))
dp.enable_features("contrib")
laplace without contrib: OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("contrib")
The helper refusal runs a call and returns the type and message of the exception. Every flag gives the same message, which names the flag and the call that enables it. So to find which calls of a script depend on a flag, run the script with that flag off.
The second flag is honest-but-curious. It gates constructors whose guarantee depends on the correctness of your arguments, mainly the plugins of Plugins. For example, make_user_measurement takes a privacy map as a Python function, and the library cannot check that the function tells the truth. The name describes the adversary the flag assumes, who is honest when building the measurement and only curious when reading its outputs. The script builds the smallest possible plugin, which releases its input unchanged and claims a privacy loss equal to the distance between inputs.
def plugin_measurement() -> dp.Measurement:
    """A plugin measurement whose privacy map is only a claim: the library cannot check `identity_map`."""
    return dp.m.make_user_measurement(
        dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False),
        dp.absolute_distance(T=float),
        dp.max_divergence(),
        function=identity,
        privacy_map=identity_map,
    )
plugin without honest-but-curious: OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
plugin with honest-but-curious: map(1.0)=1.0
With the flag on, the plugin reports whatever its map says, here a loss of 1 at distance 1, and nobody verified that number. So turn the flag on where you write and prove plugins, never where an untrusted analyst submits queries, because such an analyst could register a map that claims any loss. The same flag gates OnceFrame.lazy(), which gives back a released Polars plan that could run twice.
The third flag is idealized-numerics, which marks components whose proof assumes exact arithmetic. In 0.16.0 none of the constructors in this book needs it. The float Laplace mechanism and the float sums above build with the flag off, because their proofs account for rounding. The older name of the flag, floating-point, still works and gives a warning.
float laplace without idealized-numerics: no error
enable_features("floating-point"): DeprecationWarning: "floating-point" is deprecated. Use "idealized-numerics" instead.
assert_features("idealized-numerics") with the alias on: no error
assert_features("idealized-numerics") after disabling it: OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "idealized-numerics", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("idealized-numerics")
assert_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious"): OpenDPException: Attempted to use function that requires "contrib", "honest-but-curious", but not enabled. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/api/user-guide/#feature-listing, then call enable_features("contrib", "honest-but-curious")
The last three lines use dp.assert_features, which raises the error of a gated constructor without building anything. Every gated constructor calls it first. At the top of a script, one such line also states every flag that the script relies on. The fourth flag, rust-stack-trace, changes no guarantee, because it only adds the Rust frames to an error message, as the section on reading an exception shows.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.3 What lies outside the guarantee
The guarantee covers what happens to the data inside a measurement, and four things happen outside it in every analysis. The first is loading the data, which the documentation leaves to a trusted curator. One reason is that a CSV reader infers the type of each column from its values. The script reads three two-row files that differ in one value, then a longer file whose odd value comes after the rows that the inference reads.
for raw in (b"x
1
2
", b"x
1
2.5
", b"x
1
abc
"):
    print(f"csv {raw!r}: column x inferred as {pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(raw)).schema['x']}")
late_text = b"x
" + b"1
" * 200 + b"abc
"  # a text value after 200 numbers
failed = refusal(lambda: pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(late_text), infer_schema_length=100))
print(f"csv with a text value on row 201, inferred from 100 rows: {first_line(failed)}")
as_strings = pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(late_text), infer_schema=False).schema["x"]
print(f"the same file with infer_schema=False: column x read as {as_strings}")
csv b'x
1
2
': column x inferred as Int64
csv b'x
1
2.5
': column x inferred as Float64
csv b'x
1
abc
': column x inferred as String
csv with a text value on row 201, inferred from 100 rows: ComputeError: could not parse `abc` as dtype `i64` at column 'x' (column number 1)
the same file with infer_schema=False: column x read as String
So one person’s value decides whether the column is integer, float or text, and a late value decides whether the load succeeds at all. If the result of the load is visible outside, it is a release that nothing accounted for. The documentation gives two fixes. Read a format that carries its schema, as this book does with Parquet. Or read every column as text with infer_schema=False, then cast it yourself. The LFS loader in practitioner_datasets converts the CSV to Parquet once, which is the curator’s step, outside any guarantee.
The second thing outside the guarantee is public information. Every bound, imputed value, key list and margin in this book comes from the domain or from a published source. A bound read from the private data is a release of the data, and the library cannot tell the two apart.
The third is code that runs outside the context, which is why the data and the context told you to delete your reference to the frame. Collecting the frame yourself is not a query, so nothing counts it. The fourth is the error channel. Whether a query succeeds or fails is itself an output, so a failure that depends on the data is a release. OpenDP guards against this inside a query, for example by replacing some Polars arguments so that an expression cannot fail on one value. The loading step and your own code have no such guard.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
section: 15.4 The error messages you will meet
text:
15.4 The error messages you will meet
The documentation’s troubleshooting page has one entry, the type mismatch, and the earlier chapters met several more. This section gives each with its cause and its fix. The type mismatch comes first. OpenDP fixes the type of every argument from the domain of the data, and it refuses an argument of another type instead of converting it. The script puts three integers behind a context and clamps them with float bounds.
float bounds on integer data: TypeError: inferred type is f64, expected i32. See https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/getting-started/trouble-shooting.html#inferred-type-is-xxx-expected-yyy
integer bounds on integer data: scale=10.0
The message names the type it inferred from your argument and the type of the data. To fix it, pass bounds of the type of the data, (0, 10) for integers, or cast the data first. The documentation names one common cause, a scalar \(\varepsilon\) where a measurement expects an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair. To show it, the script asks an approximate measurement, built with make_approximate as in Combinators, whether it stays within a scalar budget.
check(1.0, 1.0) on an approximate measurement: TypeError: Cannot coerce a non-tuple type to a tuple
check(1.0, (1.0, 0.0)) on the same measurement: True
The privacy loss of an approximate measurement is a pair, so its budget must be a pair too, and a pure budget is the pair \((\varepsilon, 0)\). The same message comes from binary_search_param with a scalar d_out on an approximate chain (Utilities and the Context API).
The next message comes from a domain that allows missing values. The library infers a list of Python floats as a domain that may contain NaN. A clamp refuses such a domain, because NaN is neither inside nor outside a bound.
clamp on floats that may be nan: OpenDPException: FailedFunction("Domain contains nan")
impute, then clamp: scale=80.0
The fix is the one of the first chapter, impute_constant before clamp, which maps the domain to one without NaN. In Polars the same need appears as fill_null before a dp.sum.
The next message comes from mismatched domains in a chain. The >> operator checks that the output domain of the left side equals the input domain of the right side, and refuses otherwise. The script clamps to one range and then chains a sum built for a wider one.
vectors = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
clamp = vectors >> dp.t.then_clamp((0.0, 10.0))
wide_sum = dp.t.make_sum(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0.0, 100.0))), dp.symmetric_distance())
mismatch = refusal(lambda: clamp >> wide_sum)  # the clamp's output has bounds [0, 10], the sum wants [0, 100]
chained = clamp >> dp.t.then_sum()  # a partial constructor takes the clamp's output space, so they agree
clamp to [0, 10] then a sum built for [0, 100]: OpenDPException: DomainMismatch("Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
    output_domain: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 10.0], T=f64))
    input_domain:  VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 100.0], T=f64))
")
clamp to [0, 10] then then_sum(): sensitivity 10.0
The message prints both domains, so you can read that the bounds differ. The fix is the partial constructor then_sum(), which takes its input space from the output of the clamp (Transformations).
The remaining messages come from the Polars side, with the LFS behind a context of one query and a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\). The unit is the 36 rows of the data and the context.
def make_context(
    frame: pl.LazyFrame, delta: float | None = None, margins: Sequence[dp.polars.Margin] | None = None
) -> dp.Context:
    """The LFS behind a unit of 36 rows and a budget of epsilon = 1, with or without a delta, for one query."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=delta) if delta else dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON),
        split_evenly_over=1,
        margins=margins,
    )
A float sum needs a margin with max_length, for the reason of the first section. Its sensitivity includes a rounding term that grows with the number of rows, so the proof needs a public bound on that number.
float sum without a margin: OpenDPException: MakeTransformation("must specify 'max_length' in a margin with by=[]")
float sum with max_length=5,400,000: scale=2,881.04
The fix is the documentation’s margin, dp.polars.Margin(max_length=150_000 * 36). The scale is then a little above 2880, the sensitivity of the sum over \(\varepsilon = 1\) in exact arithmetic. The extra is the rounding term at 5.4 million rows. A grouped sum needs the same bound in the margin of its grouping, which is what by=[] in the message refers to.
The next three messages come from one query. The script builds a count and tries to collect it before it releases it. Then it releases the count, collects the result twice, and submits another query to a context whose one share is spent.
count_query = context.query().select(dp.len(signed=True))
before_release = refusal(lambda: count_query.collect())  # the plan has no data; only a released OnceFrame does
once = count_query.release()
dp_count = int(once.collect()["len"][0])
twice = refusal(lambda: once.collect())  # a second collection would be a second release
exhausted = refusal(lambda: context.query().select(dp.len(signed=True)).release())
count: scale=36.0 95% accuracy=108.34
collect before release: ValueError: You must call `.release()` before executing a query.
collect a OnceFrame twice: OpenDPException: FailedFunction("OnceFrame has been exhausted")
query after the budget is spent: ValueError: Privacy allowance has been exhausted
A LazyFrameQuery is a plan without data, so collect on it would compute nothing private. The library refuses anyway, so that the habit of collecting a plan never meets a frame that holds data. You can collect the OnceFrame from release only once, because the noise is drawn when the plan runs, so a second run would be a second release. The third message is the one that the first chapter ended on. None of the three is a bug to work around, so keep the DataFrame from the first collect if you need a value twice.
The last message is from Contingency tables. A contingency table whose keys or cuts cover every column has no private key set to protect, so its release spends no \(\delta\). The library refuses a budget with a \(\delta\) instead of leaving it unspent. The script uses \(\delta = 10^{-7}\), the value of the grouping chapters.
contingency table with keys for every column under (epsilon, delta): ValueError: delta (1e-07) must be zero because keys and cuts span all columns
the same table under pure epsilon: ContingencyTableQuery
So state the budget as pure \(\varepsilon\) when the keys are all public, or as the zero-concentrated budget \(\rho\) of Utility and noise. Keep \(\delta\) for the tables whose keys the library must discover. Two more messages from earlier chapters belong in this list. A plain mean is refused, because OpenDP has no proof for it. A grouping without keys or a \(\delta\) is refused, because its key set is private (Grouping).

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.5 Reading an OpenDPException
Most of the messages above came as an OpenDPException, which is how an error in the Rust core reaches Python. Its variant is the kind of error, from a fixed list such as DomainMismatch or FailedFunction, which code can match on. Its message is the text, and its raw_traceback is the Rust stack at the point of the error, which is recorded even if you do not display it. The script raises the domain mismatch again and reads the three, then switches on rust-stack-trace and prints the exception again.
try:
    _ = clamp >> wide_sum
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(f"variant: {err.variant}")
    print(f"message: {first_line(err.message or '')}")
    print(f"rust frames recorded: {err.raw_traceback is not None}")
    dp.enable_features("rust-stack-trace")
    print(str(err).strip())
    dp.disable_features("rust-stack-trace")
variant: DomainMismatch
message: Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
rust frames recorded: True
Continued Rust stack trace:
    opendp_combinators__make_chain_tt
    opendp::combinators::chain::make_chain_tt::<opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain, opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain, opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain, opendp::ffi::any::AnyMetric, opendp::ffi::any::AnyMetric, opendp::ffi::any::AnyMetric>
    opendp::combinators::chain::mismatch_error::<opendp::ffi::any::AnyDomain>
  DomainMismatch("Intermediate domains don't match. See https://github.com/opendp/opendp/discussions/297
    output_domain: VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 10.0], T=f64))
    input_domain:  VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0.0, 100.0], T=f64))
")
The frames read from the outside in: the entry point that Python called, the chaining function, and the helper that formats the mismatch. They help when the message does not say where in a long chain the library stopped, and they locate a bug in the Rust source. The list of variants may change between versions, so match on a variant only in tests you control. The errors that are not an OpenDPException come from the Python layer, a TypeError from argument conversion and a ValueError from the context and the query classes.

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.6 What a reviewer verifies
A release made with OpenDP claims that this table satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy for this privacy unit, and Table 15.1 collects the checks of that claim. The first is the unit, because an \(\varepsilon\) means nothing until you know what it protects. For example, dp.unit_of(contributions=36) protects a person only if nobody has more than 36 rows (Identifier truncation). The second is the budget, read back from the context.
The third is the flags, because with honest-but-curious the reviewer must read each privacy map that the library took on trust. The fourth is the source of each bound and key, and the fifth is what ran outside the context. The full edition’s chapter on the definition says what the finished claim must state.



Table 15.1: What a reviewer verifies before trusting a release made with OpenDP.










Check
Question
Where to look




Unit
What does one privacy unit contain, and does anyone exceed it?
privacy_unit in the context; the identifier and any truncation


Budget
What was spent, under which measure, and was any release collected twice?
context.current_privacy_loss(); one collect per OnceFrame


Features
Which flags were on, and if honest-but-curious, which maps were claimed?
the enable_features line; every make_user_* call and lazy()


Public information
Where did each bound, imputed value, key list and margin come from?
the constants of the script, traced to their sources


Outside the context
What touched the data before and after the context?
the load and its schema; any code holding the frame

title: 15  Limitations and troubleshooting
text:
15.8 References

OpenDP documentation: “Limitations” and the feature listing in the API user guide; “Troubleshooting” and “Next Steps” in Getting Started; the note on data loading in “Working with Tabular Data” and the margin and float-sum notes in “Essential Statistics”.
Casacuberta, Shoemate, Vadhan and Wagaman, “Widespread Underestimation of Sensitivity in Differentially Private Libraries and How to Fix It” (2022): the finite-precision sensitivity errors in earlier libraries, and the corrected proofs that OpenDP’s sums follow.
Mironov, “On Significance of the Least Significant Bits for Differential Privacy” (2012): the floating-point attack on the Laplace sampler.
Jin, McMurtry, Rubinstein and Ohrimenko, “Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems” (2022): timing and floating-point side channels in differential privacy libraries.
The full edition’s chapters on the definition and discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms derive the results this chapter states; the practitioner edition’s Release and governance gives the record a reviewer asks for.

title: Synthetic data
text:
The last part releases a dataset instead of a statistic. A synthetic dataset is a table of made-up rows whose statistics match those of the real table as closely as a privacy budget allows. OpenDP makes one in two steps. First it releases a contingency table, which holds the noisy counts of every combination of a few columns at a time. Then it fits a model to those noisy marginals and samples rows from it, which is post-processing and costs no more budget.
The thread of the part is that two choices decide the quality of the synthetic data: which marginals you measure, and how you split the budget among them. Contingency tables releases the marginals of a fixed workload with the Fixed algorithm. It explains keys, cuts and thresholds, and the ContingencyTable object with its error estimates. Synthetic data with AIM and MST lets the library choose the marginals, one round at a time with AIM or along a spanning tree with MST, and generates the rows. Evaluating and tuning synthetic data compares the result with the real data on the marginals, on a query outside the workload and on a downstream model. It also shows how the budget and the workload change the result.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




Contingency tables
How do I release the noisy counts of a set of marginals, and what does the table object hold?


Synthetic data with AIM and MST
How do I let the library choose the marginals, and how do I generate synthetic rows?


Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
How good is the synthetic data, and what changes it?






At the end of this part you can generate a private synthetic copy of a table, state its guarantee, and measure how far it is from the original.

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.1 From grouped counts to marginals
Suppose you want to publish a whole table, such as how many people of each age group usually work each number of hours, by employment status and sex. A contingency table is that table, with a count for every combination of the values of several columns. Grouping released one for two columns, and this chapter asks what changes with four columns, or forty. The answer is that you release a few marginals, the same counts for two or three columns at a time, and fit one model that agrees with all of them. The model then answers any count over those columns, consistently, from the budget already spent.
The chapter follows the documentation’s page on contingency tables. You will set up a context under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) and say which columns have known keys or cut points. Then you will release a fixed workload of marginals and read the ContingencyTable that comes back. At the end you will read a projection of the table against its error bar and add a marginal that the first release left out.
The script opendp_contingency_tables.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with mbi 1.1.0, the Private-PGM version that OpenDP pins, on the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample. The budgets, scales, thresholds, keys and error bars it prints are the same on every run. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the page shows the released counts in one block marked as one run.
The grouped counts of Grouping fail in two ways as you add columns. The first is size, because each column multiplies the number of cells by its number of values, and the four raw columns of this sample already make 4,648 cells. The second is noise. The noise on a cell does not depend on how many records the cell holds. So when the same records spread over more cells, each count gets smaller while its noise stays the same. Soon most cells are noise.
A marginal is the contingency table of a subset of the columns. Once the columns are binned as below, the two-way marginal of AGE and HWUSUAL has sixteen cells, each with a count large enough to survive its noise. Several low-order marginals keep the relations between the columns that share a marginal and give up the higher-order ones. The documentation’s workload has two marginals, AGE with HWUSUAL and HWUSUAL with ILOSTAT.
Noisy marginals released separately do not agree. For example, both marginals above contain the one-way counts of HWUSUAL, and two noisy copies of the same count differ. So OpenDP fits one probability model over all the columns whose marginals come as close as possible to the noisy ones, and every count you read comes from that model.
The method of the fit is Private-PGM (McKenna, Sheldon and Miklau, 2019), in the mbi package. Its model is a graphical model with one factor per measured marginal, fitted by mirror descent, a gradient method that keeps the model a valid distribution at every step. The fit sees only the noisy marginals, so it is post-processing and costs no budget (the full edition’s chapter on query release).
Install the extra with pip install 'opendp[mbi]', which brings mbi 1.1.0, and the documentation’s code then runs as written. Every algorithm fits its model with mbi.estimation.mirror_descent at the default of 1,000 steps, and the check at the end of the chapter asks whether that is enough on this data.

title: 16  Contingency tables
section: 16.2 The context under zCDP, with a delta
text:
16.2 The context under zCDP, with a delta
The context is the one of Assessing utility and choosing the noise, with a larger budget. The privacy unit is the book’s 36 contributions per person (the data and the context). The budget is a privacy parameter \(\rho\) of 0.2 under zCDP, which bounds the privacy loss on average, with a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\) for the stable keys. The two queries of the chapter take \(\rho = 0.1\) and \(\rho = 0.05\), so part of the budget stays unspent.
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dp.Context:
    """The context: 36 contributions per person, rho = 0.2 of zCDP with delta = 1e-7, spent query by query."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # a person answers in at most 36 quarters
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=RHO, delta=DELTA),  # the delta pays for the stable keys of ILOSTAT
    )
privacy unit: (SymmetricDistance(), 36)
privacy loss: (Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence), (0.2, 1e-07))
The budget is under zCDP because a contingency table is many counts released together. Under zCDP the Gaussian noise on all of them composes by adding their values of \(\rho\). That sum grows more slowly than the values of \(\varepsilon\) of pure differential privacy would (Combinators, and the full edition’s chapter on concentrated differential privacy). A budget in \(\varepsilon\) also works, with Laplace noise, but then the error bars below are only approximate.
The \(\delta\) is there because one column, ILOSTAT, has neither keys nor cuts, so its keys come from the data by the stable-keys release of Grouping. A key is shown only when its noisy count clears a threshold, set so that one person alone reaches it with probability at most \(\delta\). The slack pays for that threshold and for nothing else, and the library enforces this in both directions. It refuses a \(\delta\) when every column has keys or cuts, and it refuses \(\delta = 0\) when a column has neither. The script provokes both refusals on this data.
delta with keys for every column: delta (1e-07) must be zero because keys and cuts span all columns
no delta with ILOSTAT unkeyed: delta (0.0) must be nonzero because keys and cuts don't span all columns
The snippet shows the first refusal on a toy frame. It also shows that when every column has keys, nothing is spent on discovering keys, so the query reports no one-way scale or threshold.
import opendp.prelude as dp
import polars as pl

dp.enable_features("contrib")
frame = pl.LazyFrame({"SEX": [1, 2, 1, 2]})
fixed = dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(("SEX",))])
unit = dp.unit_of(contributions=1)
pure = dp.Context.compositor(data=frame, privacy_unit=unit, privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=0.1), split_evenly_over=1)
query = pure.query().contingency_table(keys={"SEX": [1, 2]}, algorithm=fixed)
print(query.oneway_scale, query.oneway_threshold)  # None None
slack = dp.loss_of(rho=0.1, delta=1e-7)
approximate = dp.Context.compositor(data=frame, privacy_unit=unit, privacy_loss=slack, split_evenly_over=1)
try:
    approximate.query().contingency_table(keys={"SEX": [1, 2]}, algorithm=fixed)
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)  # delta (1e-07) must be zero because keys and cuts span all columns

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.3 Keys and cuts
The model needs a fixed, finite set of values for every column, because its cells are indexed by them. OpenDP takes that set from one of three places. For a categorical column you pass keys, the public list of its values, as keys={"SEX": [1, 2]} from the survey’s codebook. For a numeric column you pass cuts, the public bin edges, as cuts={"AGE": [20, 40, 60]}, which make four left-open intervals, from (-inf, 20.0] to (60.0, inf]. For a column with neither, here ILOSTAT, the library spends part of the budget on stable keys, the values whose noisy counts clear the threshold.
Each of the three sources can miss values, and the library handles every miss the same way. A value outside the key list, such as a code 3 in SEX, becomes null, and so does a stable key with too small a count. So null stands for “something else”, and a true null in the data joins it. To keep true nulls apart, recode them to a value of their own with with_columns before the query, as the documentation advises. A cut column has no null bin, so a null AGE or HWUSUAL lands in the last bin. The check at the end confirms that on the 255 rows without an age and the 20,819 without usual hours.
The codebook of ILOSTAT lists six codes, from 1 for working to 9 for a child under 15. Codes 4 and 5 do not occur in this sample, so the stable keys should find four. Then null is the cell of the two missing codes, with no rows behind it.

title: 16  Contingency tables
section: 16.4 The Fixed algorithm and its workload
text:
16.4 The Fixed algorithm and its workload
dp.mbi.Fixed releases a workload you name in advance, as a list of Count queries, one per marginal. It is the right tool when you already know which relations you need, while the algorithms of the next chapter choose the marginals themselves. The query names the columns, the keys and cuts, and the algorithm.
def workload_query(context: dp.Context) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """The documentation's query: keys for SEX, cuts for AGE and HWUSUAL, stable keys for ILOSTAT, two counts."""
    return (
        context.query(rho=TABLE_RHO, delta=DELTA)
        .select("SEX", "AGE", "HWUSUAL", "ILOSTAT")
        .contingency_table(
            keys={"SEX": [1, 2]},  # public: the codebook's two codes
            cuts={"AGE": [20, 40, 60], "HWUSUAL": [1, 20, 40]},  # left-open bins: (-inf, 20], (20, 40], ...
            algorithm=dp.mbi.Fixed(
                queries=[dp.mbi.Count(("AGE", "HWUSUAL")), dp.mbi.Count(("HWUSUAL", "ILOSTAT"))],
                oneway_split=ONEWAY_SPLIT,  # the share of rho for the one-way marginal of ILOSTAT
            ),
        )
    )
The budget of the query has two parts. A share oneway_split goes to the one-way marginals of the columns without keys, which give the stable keys of ILOSTAT. The rest goes to the workload, equally over its counts unless you give them weights. By default Fixed takes half the budget times the fraction of columns without keys, here a half of a quarter. The documentation sets this one eighth explicitly, and the script prints the split.
oneway split: 0.125 of rho=0.1 -> rho=0.0125 one-way, rho=0.04375 per count
oneway scale: 227.68  oneway threshold: 1364
Read the two attributes before you release. The scale is the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise on the one-way counts of ILOSTAT. The threshold is the count that a noisy key must exceed to be kept. Both follow from the privacy unit. One person’s 36 rows can all carry the same status, so a person changes one count by up to 36, which is the sensitivity of the one-way marginal. The Gaussian scale that spends \(\rho\) on a count of sensitivity \(\Delta\) is \(\Delta / \sqrt{2\rho}\) (Assessing utility and choosing the noise), as the script checks for both parts of the budget.
scale from the formula 36 / sqrt(2 x 0.0125): 227.68
scale of each count of the workload, 36 / sqrt(2 x 0.04375): 121.70
So each cell of the two measured marginals carries Gaussian noise with standard deviation 121.70. The threshold 1364 is set as in Grouping. At scale 227.68, a key held by one person alone, in all 36 of their rows, clears it with probability at most \(\delta\). The sensitivity 36 is the price of the privacy unit, and a truncation to one row per person and year (Identifier truncation) would lower it.

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.5 The released table
table = query.release()
ilostat_std = table.std(("ILOSTAT",))
ilostat_accuracy = dp.gaussian_scale_to_accuracy(ilostat_std, alpha=ALPHA)
The release returns a ContingencyTable. It holds the key sets that the model was fitted on, the cuts, the thresholds that produced any stable keys, and the data type of the keys of each column.
keys: SEX=[1, 2, null]  AGE=[(-inf, 20.0], (20.0, 40.0], (40.0, 60.0], (60.0, inf]]  HWUSUAL=[(-inf, 1.0], (1.0, 20.0], (20.0, 40.0], (40.0, inf]]  ILOSTAT=[1, 2, 3, 9, null]
cuts: AGE=[20.0, 40.0, 60.0]  HWUSUAL=[1.0, 20.0, 40.0]
thresholds: {'ILOSTAT': 1364}
schema: {'SEX': Int64, 'AGE': String, 'HWUSUAL': String, 'ILOSTAT': Int64}
Every key set that is not a cut set ends in null, the cell for values outside the keys. So SEX has one, although the data hold only 1 and 2. The stable keys of ILOSTAT are the four codes with rows, plus null. The schema shows that a cut column now holds strings, the bin labels, so a query on the table names bins and not numbers.
The method project sums the model over every column except the ones you name, and returns the counts as an array in the order of the keys. The method project_melted returns them as a data frame. Both are post-processing. You can project onto any set of columns, even ones that no marginal measured, which the next section shows is a mixed blessing.
The method std estimates the standard deviation of a projection, and dp.gaussian_scale_to_accuracy turns it into an error bar. Projecting a two-way marginal onto one of its columns sums four noisy cells, so the standard deviation doubles, from 121.70 to 243.40. So with probability 0.95, each count of ILOSTAT is within 477.06 of the truth. That estimate leaves out the one-way marginal of ILOSTAT, because it measured only the released keys, and OpenDP counts no cell-wise precision for such a measurement. The column HWUSUAL sits in both measured marginals, and the two estimates combine by their inverse variances to 181.42.
std ILOSTAT: 243.40  95% accuracy: 477.06
std AGE x HWUSUAL: 121.70  95% accuracy: 238.53
std HWUSUAL: 181.42  95% accuracy: 355.58

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.6 Adaptive estimation
SEX has keys, but no marginal of the workload contains it. The model knows the total number of rows and nothing about how they split by sex. So it spreads the total evenly over the three keys, and std refuses to put a bar on that.
std SEX: attrs (('SEX',)) are not covered by the query set
A second query repairs this without starting over. Passing the released table as table= tells the library to keep its keys, cuts, marginals and model, measure the new marginals, and fit the model again. Every column now has keys, including the ones that the first release found, so this query must carry \(\delta = 0\) and spends nothing on key discovery.
def sex_query(context: dp.Context, table: dp.mbi.ContingencyTable) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """A second query that adds the marginal of SEX to the released table's model; every key is known, so delta = 0."""
    return (
        context.query(rho=SEX_RHO, delta=0.0)
        .select("SEX")
        .contingency_table(
            table=table,  # keep the keys, cuts, marginals and model of the first release
            algorithm=dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(("SEX",))]),
        )
    )
The new marginal is a one-way count at \(\rho = 0.05\) with the same sensitivity of 36, so its scale is 113.84. The three cells of SEX then have an error bar of 223.13. The model now has four marginals, and the context has spent \(\rho = 0.15\) of its 0.2. The budget of the second query was chosen after seeing the first table, which is the adaptive composition of Combinators. The new fit starts from the first model and runs its own 1,000 steps of mirror descent.
std SEX after the second query: 113.84  95% accuracy: 223.13
marginals in the model: [('ILOSTAT',), ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL'), ('HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT'), ('SEX',)]
privacy loss spent: (0.15, 1e-07)

title: 16  Contingency tables
section: 16.7 Checking the release against the truth
text:
16.7 Checking the release against the truth
The data are public, so the script computes the true values that the table estimates. Polars gives the true one-way counts of ILOSTAT and the true AGE by HWUSUAL table for the documentation’s cuts. Every null age or null hours goes in the last bin, as the library places them.
true ILOSTAT counts: 1=1,517,011  2=155,661  3=1,450,283  9=688,977
true AGE x HWUSUAL (a null AGE or HWUSUAL counts in the last bin):
  AGE (-inf, 20.0]: (-inf, 1.0]=2,733  (1.0, 20.0]=13,651  (20.0, 40.0]=95,686  (40.0, inf]=1,051,617
  AGE (20.0, 40.0]: (-inf, 1.0]=1,441  (1.0, 20.0]=31,415  (20.0, 40.0]=370,616  (40.0, inf]=258,601
  AGE (40.0, 60.0]: (-inf, 1.0]=1,285  (1.0, 20.0]=46,743  (20.0, 40.0]=437,820  (40.0, inf]=309,224
  AGE (60.0, inf]: (-inf, 1.0]=1,502  (1.0, 20.0]=28,084  (20.0, 40.0]=122,405  (40.0, inf]=1,039,109
The releases of one run follow, to read against the error bars above. They show more than the noise.
released (one run):
  ILOSTAT 1: 1,515,589  (true 1,517,011, off by -1,422)
  ILOSTAT 2: 155,622  (true 155,661, off by -39)
  ILOSTAT 3: 1,450,332  (true 1,450,283, off by +49)
  ILOSTAT 9: 688,890  (true 688,977, off by -87)
  ILOSTAT null: 1,142  (true 0, off by +1,142)
  AGE x HWUSUAL largest |released - true|: 521  (accuracy 238.53)
  at AGE (60.0, inf] HWUSUAL (40.0, inf]: 1,038,588  (true 1,039,109)
  last bin of both, the nulls' cell: 1,038,588  (true 1,039,109, off by -521)
  SEX before the second query: 1,270,525 1,270,525 1,270,525  (uniform)
  SEX after: 1: 1,828,537  (true 1,828,992)  2: 1,982,506  (true 1,982,940)  null: 610  (true 0)
  ILOSTAT after the second query:
    ILOSTAT 1: 1,516,288  (true 1,517,011, off by -723)
    ILOSTAT 2: 155,608  (true 155,661, off by -53)
    ILOSTAT 3: 1,450,301  (true 1,450,283, off by +18)
    ILOSTAT 9: 688,867  (true 688,977, off by -110)
    ILOSTAT null: 590  (true 0, off by +590)
Start with the cells that the noise alone explains. The largest of the sixteen two-way errors is 521 rows, past twice the bar of 238.53 per cell but inside three times it. It sits in the last bin of both columns, which holds the rows without usual hours or age, so the run confirms where the library puts a null. The null keys of ILOSTAT and SEX have no rows behind them, but their estimates are positive, because a fitted distribution cannot go negative. Keep that in mind for a cell whose truth may be zero.
The fit, not the noise, explains the other errors. The working code 1 of ILOSTAT came out 1,422 rows short, past twice its bar of 477.06. The empty null key holds 1,142 rows. The fit starts from the uniform model, so null begins with a fifth of all rows. A key with no rows is the slowest cell to fit, because the model can empty it only in the limit. So 1,000 steps leave about a thousand rows in it, and those rows are missing from the other keys.
The second query shows the same thing in SEX. Its fit starts from the first model, in which the null key of SEX holds a third of all rows. After 1,000 steps that key still holds 610 rows, more than twice its bar. So the two real keys are short by 455 and 434 rows. The same steps continued to fit ILOSTAT, whose working code is now 723 rows short.
To settle it, the script fits the four released marginals of the second table again from scratch, with 10,000 steps of mbi.estimation.mirror_descent instead of the default 1,000. That touches no data, so it is post-processing and a dev-time check, never part of a release.
  the same marginals refitted at 10,000 steps (dev time, post-processing):
    ILOSTAT 1: 1,516,829  (true 1,517,011, off by -182)
    ILOSTAT 2: 155,587  (true 155,661, off by -74)
    ILOSTAT 3: 1,450,277  (true 1,450,283, off by -6)
    ILOSTAT 9: 688,859  (true 688,977, off by -118)
    ILOSTAT null: 103  (true 0, off by +103)
    SEX: 1: 1,828,829  (true 1,828,992)  2: 1,982,798  (true 1,982,940)  null: 27  (true 0)
    AGE x HWUSUAL largest |refit - true|: 295  (accuracy 238.53)
With more steps, the null key of ILOSTAT keeps 103 rows and that of SEX 27, inside their bars. Code 1 is within 182 rows of the truth and each real key of SEX within 163. The largest two-way error is 295 rows, inside three times its bar. So a fit that stops early biases the empty cells upward and the largest ones downward, and nothing in the release warns you. A dev-time check against public or historical data is how you notice it.
The test behind the script holds each two-way cell and each count of the longer fit within three times its bar. For the default fit, it checks that each null holds less than a tenth of a percent of the rows. It also checks that each real key is within three times its bar plus the rows left in null.

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.8 Summary



Table 16.1: The calls and concepts of a contingency-table release, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




dp.loss_of(rho=0.2, delta=1e-7)
A zCDP budget with a slack for stable keys
Gaussian noise composes tightly over many marginals; the \(\delta\) is needed exactly when a column has neither keys nor cuts


keys={"SEX": [1, 2]}
The public values of a categorical column
Values outside the list become null


cuts={"AGE": [20, 40, 60]}
Left-open bins of a numeric column
Three cuts make four bins; a null lands in the last one


A column with neither
Stable keys, bought with oneway_split of the budget
Rare values fall below the threshold and join null


dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(...)], oneway_split=1/8)
A workload named in advance
The rest of the budget is shared equally over the counts, or by their weights


query.oneway_scale, query.oneway_threshold
The noise and the cut-off of the key discovery
Read them before releasing; both are None when every column is keyed


table.keys, table.cuts, table.thresholds, table.schema
What the model was fitted on
Cut columns come back as bin labels, not numbers


table.project, table.project_melted
Any count over the table’s columns, from the model
Post-processing; a column no marginal covers comes back uniform


table.std with dp.gaussian_scale_to_accuracy
The error bar of a covered projection
Raises for an uncovered projection; a cell near zero is biased upward


contingency_table(table=table, ...)
Adds marginals to an existing model
Every key is then known, so \(\delta = 0\)


mbi.estimation.mirror_descent(domain, marginals, iters=...)
Refits the released marginals with more steps
Post-processing; the default 1,000 steps leave rows in the empty null keys on this data, so check the fit on public data

title: 16  Contingency tables
text:
16.9 References

OpenDP documentation: “Contingency Tables” in Getting Started, and the opening of “Synthetic Data”, which lists the algorithms and the rules for null values.
McKenna, Sheldon and Miklau, “Graphical-model based estimation and inference for differential privacy” (2019): Private-PGM, the model that one consistent table is fitted from, and the mirror-descent fit.
Bun and Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (2016): zCDP and the Gaussian mechanism under it.
The full edition’s chapters on query release, sensitivity and concentrated differential privacy derive the results this chapter states.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.1 When you do not know the questions
Contingency tables released the marginals you asked for, which works when you know the questions in advance. The analyst of a synthetic dataset usually does not, and a workload that guesses wrong leaves the relations they care about to chance. So this chapter lets the library choose. The AIM algorithm picks its marginals one round at a time, each time the one that its current model gets most wrong. The MST algorithm picks a spanning tree of column pairs in one step. Both fit a model to the noisy marginals, and synthesize() turns the model into rows, which is post-processing and costs nothing.
The chapter follows the documentation’s synthetic-data page and the docstrings of dp.mbi.AIM, dp.mbi.MST, dp.mbi.Sequential and ContingencyTable.synthesize. You will release three tables over four survey columns and read which marginals each algorithm chose. Then you will generate a synthetic frame of 3.8 million rows, state the guarantee, and compare the synthetic marginals with the real ones. That comparison shows a problem with nulls, which you will fix.
The script opendp_aim_and_mst.py runs everything on the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample with OpenDP 0.16.0 and mbi 1.1.0, the Private-PGM version that OpenDP pins, with JAX on the CPU. The noise scales, the threshold, the budget arithmetic, the conversion to \(\varepsilon\) and the facts about the data are the same on every run. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the chosen marginals, the counts, the rows and the distances to the real data change. The page shows them in blocks marked as one run. The whole script takes about 75 seconds.
A fixed workload spends the budget on the marginals you name and on nothing else. For a pair of columns you did not name, the model answers as if the two columns were independent, as SEX came out uniform in the previous chapter. With four columns you could name every pair and every triple. But the budget would then spread over ten marginals, most of which the model fits well anyway. The question is how to spend the budget where the model is wrong.
AIM answers it adaptively. It first measures the one-way marginal of every column with half the budget, which also releases the keys of a column without keys. Then it fits a model and runs rounds. Each round scores every candidate marginal of up to three columns by how far the model’s version is from the true one, minus what measuring it would cost in noise. Candidates that overlap the workload weigh more, so the three-way marginals, which are the workload itself, weigh most.
A noisy selection with a tenth of the round’s budget picks one candidate, by the report-noisy-max form of the exponential mechanism (the full edition’s chapter on selection). The other nine tenths measure the chosen marginal with Gaussian noise, and AIM fits the model again.
The budget per round adapts. It starts at the budget divided by the number of rounds. When a measurement moves the model by less than its noise, the round taught little, so the next round gets four times the share. The rounds stop when a privacy filter finds the budget spent. The rounds argument sets the number of planned rounds, by default sixteen per column, which is 64 here, and the script uses 10 so that a release takes seconds. The max_size argument caps the memory of the model in megabytes, which never binds with four small columns.
The queries argument is either the largest number of columns of a candidate, 3 by default, or a workload of weighted dp.mbi.Count objects. The measure_split of 0.9 is the share of each round that goes to measuring. MST has the same split and one argument of its own, num_selections (Section 17.3).

import opendp.prelude as dp

print(aim.queries, aim.measure_split, aim.max_size, aim.rounds)  # 3 0.9 80.0 None

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.2 The AIM release
The context is the documentation’s, with three times the budget because this chapter releases three tables. The privacy unit is 36 contributions per person, as in the data and the context. The budget is a privacy parameter \(\rho\) of 0.3 under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), with Gaussian noise. The parameter bounds the privacy loss on average (the full edition’s chapter on concentrated differential privacy (DP)). The slack \(\delta\) of \(3 \times 10^{-7}\) pays for releasing the keys of ILOSTAT, which the query does not name.
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dp.Context:
    """The context: a privacy unit of 36 rows, a budget of rho = 0.3 with delta = 3e-7, one share per release."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # neighbours add or remove one person's 36 rows
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=RHO, delta=DELTA),  # zCDP with Gaussian noise; delta pays for ILOSTAT's keys
    )
Every release goes through one function, because the three queries differ only in the algorithm. The query takes a third of the budget, \(\rho = 0.1\) with \(\delta = 10^{-7}\). It selects the documentation’s four columns, gives the keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL, and leaves ILOSTAT to the threshold. The fill argument is for later.
def table_query(context: dp.Context, algorithm: Algorithm, fill: bool = False) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """The documentation's contingency-table query at rho = 0.1 and delta = 1e-7, with the algorithm plugged in."""
    query = context.query(rho=RHO_QUERY, delta=DELTA_QUERY)
    if fill:
        query = query.with_columns(fill_nulls())  # a row-by-row transformation before the table
    return query.select(*COLUMNS).contingency_table(
        keys=KEYS,  # public categories of SEX; ILOSTAT's are released with the threshold
        cuts=CUTS,  # bins for the two numeric columns
        algorithm=algorithm,
    )
The first release uses AIM with ten rounds. Before the release, the query reports the scale and the threshold of its one-way step, which cost nothing to read.
aim_query = table_query(context, dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS))
oneway_scale, oneway_threshold = aim_query.oneway_scale, aim_query.oneway_threshold
table_aim, seconds_aim = timed_release(aim_query)
privacy unit: (SymmetricDistance(), 36)
privacy loss: (Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence), (0.3, 3e-07))
query budget: rho=0.1 delta=1e-07
aim: oneway scale=227.6840 threshold=1364
aim: rho per one-way marginal=0.0125  scale 36/sqrt(2 rho)=227.6840
aim: rounds=10  rho per round=0.0050  measure=0.0045  select=0.0005  scale of a round's marginal=379.4733
aim keys ILOSTAT: [1, 2, 3, 9, None]  thresholds: {'ILOSTAT': 1364}
The scales follow from the budget split. Half of the query’s \(\rho\) goes to the one-way step, where AIM measures all four one-way marginals, so each gets 0.0125. One person changes the cells of a marginal by at most 36 rows in all, possibly all in one cell. So the sensitivity in the Euclidean norm is 36. Write \(\Delta_2\) for that sensitivity and \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise. The mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2}{\sqrt{2\rho}}, \tag{17.1}\] and that formula gives the 227.68 the query reports.
The other half of the share is divided over the ten rounds. Nine tenths of the 0.005 of a round goes to measuring, and the formula gives 379.47 for the marginal of a round. The threshold of 1364 is the noisy count that a category of ILOSTAT must clear to be released. The keys are the four codes in the data plus the null that stands for anything else.
aim release (one run): 13.4 s
aim measured: ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=189.74
aim measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'ILOSTAT') std=379.47
aim measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL') std=379.47
aim measured: ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=379.47
The marginals attribute of the table holds every measurement with its clique, the columns it spans, and its noise. In this run AIM measured all four three-way marginals before any pair, as the weights predict. One of them appears twice, the second time at half the scale, which is the adaptive rule at work. A round had moved the model by less than its noise, so the next round took four times the share, which was all that was left. So there were seven measurements and not ten. Another run chooses differently, so read this list after every release.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
section: 17.3 A spanning tree of pairs with MST
text:
17.3 A spanning tree of pairs with MST
MST, the mechanism that won the 2018 NIST synthetic-data contest, is simpler than AIM. After the same one-way step it scores only pairs of columns, by how far the model’s version is from the true one. Then it picks pairs one at a time by noisy maximum, each time among the pairs that join two columns not yet connected. With four columns that gives three pairs, which form a tree that spans every column, hence the name. The num_selections argument sets how many pairs to pick, by default one fewer than the number of columns. Then MST measures all the selected pairs at once with nine tenths of the remaining budget, and fits the model.
mst_query = table_query(context, dp.mbi.MST())
table_mst, seconds_mst = timed_release(mst_query)
mst: oneway scale=227.6840 threshold=1364
mst: pairs=3  rho per pair=0.0150  scale of a pair=207.8461
mst release (one run): 3.3 s
mst measured: ('HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=207.85
mst measured: ('AGE', 'ILOSTAT') std=207.85
mst measured: ('SEX', 'ILOSTAT') std=207.85
mst pairs form a spanning tree: True
The one-way step is identical, so its scale and threshold are the same. The three pairs share nine tenths of the remaining budget, 0.015 each, and the formula gives 207.85. So each pair is measured more precisely than a round of AIM, because MST commits to three measurements where AIM keeps budget back for rounds it may need. In this run the tree is a star on ILOSTAT, the column most related to the other three. The script checks that the pairs connect all four columns without a cycle, as the selection guarantees.
